school-c10-maths-a.title: Class 10 Mathematics — Part A (Ch 1–7)
school-c10-maths-a.description: Class 10 Mathematics chapter by chapter: Real Numbers to Coordinate Geometry, with solved examples, common mistakes, quizzes and board-style chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Real Numbers
courses.summary: Prime factorisation and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF and LCM, and proofs that numbers like √2, √3 and √5 are irrational — explained step by step with board-style solved examples.
outcomes: Learners can state and use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
Learners can find HCF and LCM by prime factorisation and use HCF × LCM = product of two numbers
Learners can prove that √2, √3, √5 and expressions like 3 + 2√5 are irrational
Learners can solve word problems on HCF and LCM

scenes.text: Riya's teacher writes 3150 on the board and asks: can you break it into building blocks that cannot be broken further?
Riya splits 3150 = 2 × 1575, then 1575 = 3 × 525, and keeps going until only primes are left.
Her friend Arjun starts differently (3150 = 10 × 315) but ends with exactly the same primes. Why? That is today's theorem.

steps.title: Primes and composites
steps.body:
A **prime** has exactly two factors: 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 …). A **composite** number has more than two factors. 1 is neither prime nor composite.

**Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA):** every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is **unique** apart from the order of the factors.

So 3150 = 2 × 3² × 5² × 7, whichever way you start the factor tree.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — can 4ⁿ end with the digit 0?
steps.body:
**Step 1:** A number ends in 0 only if it is divisible by 10 = 2 × 5, so its prime factorisation must contain **both** 2 and 5.

**Step 2:** 4ⁿ = (2²)ⁿ = 2²ⁿ. Its only prime factor is 2.

**Step 3:** By the uniqueness in FTA, no factor 5 can ever appear.

**Conclusion:** 4ⁿ never ends with 0 for any natural number n. (The same argument works for 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ.)

steps.title: Exam habit
steps.body: Write prime factorisations in **index form** in ascending order of primes: 2⁵ × 3 × 101. It makes HCF/LCM work almost automatic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 1 as a prime factor (1 is not prime).
- Stopping too early: 143 looks prime but is 11 × 13. Test primes up to √n.
- Saying a number ends in 0 just because it is even — it also needs a factor 5.

statements.s: 1 is a prime number.
statements.why: A prime has exactly two factors; 1 has only one.

statements.s: The prime factorisation of 3150 is unique except for the order of factors.
statements.why: That is the uniqueness part of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

statements.s: 12ⁿ can end with the digit 0 for some n.
143 is a prime number.

quiz.q: Which is the prime factorisation of 140?
quiz.why: 140 = 2 × 70 = 2 × 2 × 35 = 2² × 5 × 7. The options with 14 or 4 are not full prime factorisations because 14 and 4 are composite.

quiz.q: Which number is neither prime nor composite?
quiz.why: 1 has only one factor, itself, so it is neither prime (exactly two factors) nor composite (more than two factors).

quiz.q: For which digit can 6ⁿ never end, for any natural number n?
quiz.why: 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no prime factor 5. A number ends in 0 only if it is divisible by both 2 and 5, so 6ⁿ can never end in 0.

quiz.q: 3825 in prime factor form is
quiz.why: 3825 = 5 × 765 = 5 × 5 × 153 = 5² × 9 × 17 = 3² × 5² × 17. The other options contain 51, 85 or 153, which are not prime.

quiz.q: The FTA guarantees that prime factorisation is
quiz.why: By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, a number's prime factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors. The order may change, but the primes and their powers cannot.

lessons.title: HCF and LCM by prime factorisation

scenes.text: Sonia takes 18 minutes and Ravi 12 minutes to complete one round of a circular track.
They start together at the same point in the same direction.
After how many minutes will they meet again at the start? The answer is the LCM — let us learn to find it fast.

steps.title: The method
steps.body:
Write each number as a product of primes in index form.

- **HCF** = product of the **common** primes, each raised to its **smallest** power.
- **LCM** = product of **all** primes that appear, each raised to its **greatest** power.

For any two positive integers a and b: **HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b**. This product rule does NOT hold for three numbers.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — HCF and LCM of 96 and 404
steps.body:
**Step 1:** 96 = 2⁵ × 3 and 404 = 2² × 101.

**Step 2:** Common prime: 2, smallest power 2². HCF = 4.

**Step 3:** All primes with greatest powers: 2⁵ × 3 × 101 = 9696. LCM = 9696.

**Check:** 4 × 9696 = 38784 and 96 × 404 = 38784 ✓

steps.title: Solved example 2 — three numbers 6, 72, 120
steps.body:
6 = 2 × 3, 72 = 2³ × 3², 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5.

HCF = 2¹ × 3¹ = **6**. LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = **360**.

Note: 6 × 360 = 2160 but 6 × 72 × 120 = 51840 — the product rule fails for three numbers.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — using the product rule
Back to the runners
steps.body: LCM(18, 12): 18 = 2 × 3², 12 = 2² × 3, so LCM = 2² × 3² = 36. They meet again after **36 minutes**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the greatest powers for HCF (it is the smallest).
- Using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers.
- Forgetting a prime that appears in only one number when finding LCM (101 in 404).

activity.prompt: Find the LCM of 18 and 24 (they could be the intervals, in minutes, at which two bells ring).

quiz.q: HCF of 2³ × 3² and 2² × 3³ is
quiz.why: For HCF, take each common prime with its smaller power: 2² and 3². So HCF = 2² × 3².

quiz.q: LCM of 2³ × 3² and 2² × 3³ is
quiz.why: For LCM, take every prime with its greater power: 2³ and 3³. So LCM = 2³ × 3³.

quiz.q: If HCF(a, b) = 12 and a × b = 1800, LCM(a, b) is
quiz.why: HCF × LCM = a × b, so LCM = 1800 ÷ 12 = 150.

quiz.q: HCF of two consecutive natural numbers is always
quiz.why: Any common factor of two consecutive numbers must also divide their difference, which is 1. So their HCF is always 1.

quiz.q: LCM of 6, 72 and 120 is
quiz.why: 6 = 2 × 3, 72 = 2³ × 3², 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5. Taking the highest powers gives LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

quiz.q: If two numbers are co-prime, their LCM equals
quiz.why: Co-prime numbers have HCF = 1. Since LCM = product ÷ HCF, their LCM equals their product.

scenes.text: A square tile has side 1 m. Its diagonal is √2 m.
Kabir tries to write √2 as a neat fraction like 7/5 or 141/100 — each is close, none is exact.
Instead of trying forever, mathematicians prove it is impossible. That proof is a favourite board question.

steps.title: Key facts you may quote
steps.body:
A number is **rational** if it can be written as p/q with integers p, q, q ≠ 0. Otherwise it is **irrational**.

**Theorem:** Let p be a prime. If p divides a², then p divides a (a a positive integer). This follows from FTA.

Also: rational + irrational = irrational; non-zero rational × irrational = irrational.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — prove √2 is irrational
steps.body:
**Step 1 (assume the opposite):** Suppose √2 = a/b where a, b are co-prime integers, b ≠ 0.

**Step 2:** Squaring, 2b² = a². So 2 divides a², hence 2 divides a. Write a = 2c.

**Step 3:** Then 2b² = 4c², so b² = 2c². So 2 divides b², hence 2 divides b.

**Step 4 (contradiction):** 2 divides both a and b, but they were co-prime.

**Conclusion:** our assumption is false, so √2 is irrational. (Replace 2 by 3 or 5 to prove √3, √5 irrational.)

steps.title: Solved example 2 — prove 3 + 2√5 is irrational
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Suppose 3 + 2√5 = r, a rational number.

**Step 2:** Then √5 = (r − 3)/2.

**Step 3:** The right side is rational (rationals are closed under subtraction and division by a non-zero number), so √5 would be rational.

**Step 4:** This contradicts the fact that √5 is irrational. Hence 3 + 2√5 is irrational.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — prove 1/√2 is irrational
steps.body: Suppose 1/√2 = p/q (co-prime, p ≠ 0). Then √2 = q/p, which is rational — a contradiction. So 1/√2 is irrational.

steps.title: Board-answer structure
steps.body: Always write the three moves clearly: **Assume** rational in lowest terms → **Derive** a consequence → **Contradiction** → **Conclude**. Marks are given for each move.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not stating that a and b are co-prime — without it there is no contradiction.
- Writing 'p divides a² so p divides a' for a non-prime p (false for 4: 4 divides 36 = 6², yet 4 does not divide 6).
- Thinking irrational + irrational is always irrational: √2 + (−√2) = 0.

activity.prompt: Put the steps of the proof that √3 is irrational in order.
items: Assume √3 = a/b with a, b co-prime, b ≠ 0
Square: 3b² = a², so 3 divides a² and hence a
Write a = 3c, giving b² = 3c², so 3 divides b
3 divides both a and b — contradicts co-prime
Therefore √3 is irrational

quiz.q: Which of these is irrational?
quiz.why: 7 is not a perfect square, so √7 is irrational. 22/7 and 0.25 are rational, and √16 = 4 is rational too.

quiz.q: The proof that √5 is irrational is a proof by
quiz.why: To prove √5 is irrational we assume the opposite, that it is rational, and reach a contradiction. This is proof by contradiction.

quiz.q: If p is prime and p divides a², then
quiz.why: If a prime p divides a², then p divides a. This is the key theorem used in proofs of irrationality.
√2 × √2 = 2, which is rational. So the product of two irrational numbers can be rational.
A rational number minus an irrational number is irrational, so 5 − √3 is irrational.

scenes.text: A shop has 420 kaju barfis and 130 badam barfis to stack in trays.
Each stack must hold one kind and the same number in every stack, using the fewest trays.
The best stack height is the HCF. Real problems hide HCF and LCM inside everyday words.

steps.title: Spot the clue words
steps.body:
- **HCF** problems: 'greatest/largest', 'maximum number in each group', 'cut into equal longest pieces', 'arrange in rows with the same number'.
- **LCM** problems: 'least/smallest', 'meet again', 'ring together again', 'minimum number divisible by'.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — sweets in stacks
steps.body:
HCF(420, 130): 420 = 2² × 3 × 5 × 7, 130 = 2 × 5 × 13. HCF = 2 × 5 = **10**.

Each stack has 10 barfis; number of stacks = 42 + 13 = **55**, the least number of trays.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — army band
steps.body:
An army contingent of 616 members marches behind a band of 32 members in the same number of columns. Maximum number of columns = HCF(616, 32).

616 = 2³ × 7 × 11, 32 = 2⁵. HCF = 2³ = **8 columns**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — smallest number with remainders
steps.body:
Find the smallest number which when divided by 12, 16 and 24 leaves remainder 5.

LCM(12, 16, 24): 12 = 2² × 3, 16 = 2⁴, 24 = 2³ × 3 → LCM = 2⁴ × 3 = 48. Required number = 48 + 5 = **53**.

steps.title: Extra: Euclid's division algorithm
steps.body: Some state boards still teach it: to find HCF(a, b) with a > b, write a = bq + r (0 ≤ r < b), then repeat with (b, r) until r = 0; the last divisor is the HCF. Example: 455 = 42 × 10 + 35, 42 = 35 × 1 + 7, 35 = 7 × 5 + 0 → HCF = 7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using LCM where the question says 'maximum/greatest size' (that is HCF).
- Forgetting to add the remainder at the end in remainder problems.
- Stopping at the HCF when the question asks for the number of groups or stacks.

activity.prompt: Decide: is each problem solved with HCF or LCM?

items.text: Longest tape that measures 7 m, 3.85 m and 12.95 m exactly
When will three traffic lights change together again?
Maximum number of students who can share 1001 pens and 910 pencils equally
Largest square tile for a 6 m × 9 m floor
Two buses leave every 20 and 25 min; when together again?

quiz.q: Largest number dividing 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8 respectively is
quiz.why: The divisor must exceed the remainders. Subtract them: 70 − 5 = 65 and 125 − 8 = 117. HCF(65, 117) = 13 (65 = 5 × 13, 117 = 9 × 13), and 13 > 8.

quiz.q: Two bells toll every 6 and 8 seconds. They toll together again after
quiz.why: The bells toll together at the common multiples of 6 and 8. LCM(6, 8) = 24, so they toll together again after 24 seconds.

quiz.q: Maximum number of students sharing 1001 pens and 910 pencils equally is
quiz.why: The maximum number of students is HCF(1001, 910). 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 and 910 = 2 × 5 × 7 × 13, so HCF = 7 × 13 = 91.

quiz.q: Using Euclid's algorithm, HCF(135, 225) is
quiz.why: 225 = 135 × 1 + 90; 135 = 90 × 1 + 45; 90 = 45 × 2 + 0. The last non-zero divisor, 45, is the HCF.

quiz.q: Smallest number that when divided by 12, 16, 24 leaves remainder 5 is
quiz.why: LCM(12, 16, 24) = 48. The smallest number leaving remainder 5 is LCM + 5 = 48 + 5 = 53.

questions.q: The prime factorisation of 156 is
questions.why: 156 = 2 × 78 = 2 × 2 × 39 = 2² × 3 × 13. The options with 78, 39 or 4 are not complete prime factorisations.

questions.q: HCF(26, 91) is
questions.why: 26 = 2 × 13 and 91 = 7 × 13. The only common prime factor is 13, so HCF = 13.

questions.q: LCM(26, 91) is
Which is irrational?
questions.why: 11 is not a perfect square, so √11 is irrational. 0.3333… = 1/3, 7/9 and √25 = 5 are rational.

questions.q: If HCF(96, 404) = 4, then LCM(96, 404) is
Assertion (A): 6ⁿ can never end with digit 0. Reason (R): 6ⁿ has no prime factor 5.
options: Both A and R true; R explains A
Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true. A number ends in 0 only if it has both 2 and 5 as factors, and 6ⁿ has no factor 5, so R explains A.

questions.q: HCF of the smallest prime and the smallest composite number is
questions.why: The smallest prime is 2 and the smallest composite number is 4. HCF(2, 4) = 2.

questions.q: If a = 2³ × 3 and b = 2 × 3 × 5, then HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) equals
questions.why: HCF × LCM = a × b. Here a = 2³ × 3 = 24 and b = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30, so the product is 24 × 30 = 720.

questions.q: Case: Three friends visit a library every 4, 6 and 10 days respectively and met there today. They will next all meet after
questions.why: They meet again after a number of days that is a multiple of 4, 6 and 10. LCM(4, 6, 10) = 60, so after 60 days.

questions.q: In the proof that √2 is irrational we assume √2 = a/b where a and b are
questions.why: We assume √2 = a/b with a and b co-prime integers and b ≠ 0. Being in lowest terms matters, because the proof leads to both being even, a contradiction.

questions.q: Which statement is false?
options: Sum of a rational and an irrational is irrational
HCF × LCM = product for two numbers
Product of two irrationals is always irrational
questions.why: √3 × √3 = 3, which is rational, so the statement that the product of two irrationals is always irrational is false. The other statements are true.

questions.q: The largest number that divides 245 and 1029 leaving remainder 5 in each case is
Numbers 1–10: their LCM is
questions.why: The LCM of 1 to 10 uses the highest powers of the primes: 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 = 8 × 9 × 5 × 7 = 2520.

questions.q: If LCM(x, 18) = 36 and HCF(x, 18) = 2, then x is
Minimum length of a rope that can be cut exactly into pieces of 15 cm, 24 cm and 36 cm is
questions.why: The shortest rope is the LCM of 15, 24 and 36. 15 = 3 × 5, 24 = 2³ × 3, 36 = 2² × 3², so LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360 cm.
(√2 + √3)² = 2 + 3 + 2√6 = 5 + 2√6, which is irrational. The others simplify to 1, 3 and 2/7, which are rational.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Polynomials
courses.summary: Degree and types of polynomials, what zeroes mean on a graph, the relationship between zeroes and coefficients, and building a quadratic from given zeroes — with solved board-style problems.
outcomes: Learners can identify degree and type of a polynomial
Learners can read the number of zeroes from a graph
Learners can find zeroes of a quadratic and verify sum and product relations
Learners can form a quadratic polynomial from the sum and product of its zeroes
Learners can evaluate symmetric expressions like α² + β² without finding α and β

lessons.title: Polynomials and the geometric meaning of zeroes

scenes.text: Neha kicks a ball. Its height is modelled by h(t) = −5t² + 10t, a quadratic polynomial.
When h(t) = 0, the ball is on the ground: at t = 0 and t = 2 seconds.
On a graph, those moments are exactly where the curve meets the t-axis. That is what a 'zero' looks like.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
A **polynomial** in x has terms with whole-number powers of x: p(x) = 3x² − 5x + 2.

- **Degree** = highest power: linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3).
- A **zero** of p(x) is a value k with p(k) = 0.
- 1/x, √x and x^(−2) terms are NOT allowed in a polynomial.

steps.title: Zeroes on a graph
steps.body:
The zeroes of y = p(x) are the **x-coordinates where the graph meets the x-axis**.

- Linear ax + b (a ≠ 0): a straight line, exactly one zero −b/a.
- Quadratic ax² + bx + c: a **parabola** opening up (a > 0) or down (a < 0); it can cut the x-axis at 2 points, touch it at 1 point, or miss it — so 0, 1 or 2 zeroes.
- A polynomial of degree n has **at most n** zeroes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — count zeroes from a graph
steps.body:
A graph of y = p(x) crosses the x-axis at x = −2, 0 and 3 and nowhere else.

**Answer:** p(x) has **3** zeroes: −2, 0, 3. (The y-intercept does not count; only x-axis meetings do.)

steps.title: Solved example 2 — check a zero
steps.body:
Is x = 2 a zero of p(x) = x² − 3x + 2?

p(2) = 4 − 6 + 2 = 0, so **yes**. Also p(1) = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0, so 1 is the other zero.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting points where the curve meets the **y-axis** as zeroes.
- Thinking every quadratic has two zeroes (it can have 0 or 1 real zero).
- Calling x² + 1/x a polynomial.

activity.prompt: Sort each expression by degree.

quiz.q: Degree of 5x³ − 4x² + x − 9 is
quiz.why: The degree is the highest power of x. Here the highest power is 3.

quiz.q: The graph of a quadratic polynomial is a
quiz.why: The graph of a quadratic polynomial y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola.

quiz.q: If a graph of y = p(x) touches the x-axis at exactly one point and never crosses elsewhere, p(x) has
quiz.why: The number of zeroes equals the number of points where the graph meets the x-axis. Here it touches at exactly one point, so there is 1 zero.

quiz.q: Zero of 3x − 6 is
quiz.why: 3x − 6 = 0 gives 3x = 6, so x = 2.

quiz.q: Maximum number of zeroes of a cubic polynomial is
quiz.why: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes. A cubic therefore has at most 3 zeroes.

lessons.title: Zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic

scenes.text: Kabir says: 'My two numbers add up to 2 and multiply to −8.'
Meera writes x² − 2x − 8 and factorises it: (x − 4)(x + 2).
The secret numbers are 4 and −2. The coefficients of a quadratic quietly store the sum and product of its zeroes.

steps.title: The relations
steps.body:
If α and β are zeroes of p(x) = ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0), then

- **α + β = −b/a**  (− coefficient of x ÷ coefficient of x²)
- **αβ = c/a**  (constant term ÷ coefficient of x²)

Why: ax² + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β) = ax² − a(α + β)x + aαβ; compare coefficients.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — x² + 7x + 10
steps.body:
**Step 1 (factorise):** x² + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5). Zeroes: −2 and −5.

**Step 2 (verify sum):** −2 + (−5) = −7 and −b/a = −7/1 = −7 ✓

**Step 3 (verify product):** (−2)(−5) = 10 and c/a = 10/1 = 10 ✓

steps.title: Solved example 2 — 4u² + 8u
steps.body:
4u² + 8u = 4u(u + 2), so zeroes are 0 and −2.

Sum = −2 = −8/4 ✓. Product = 0 = 0/4 ✓ (c = 0 here).

steps.title: Solved example 4 — splitting the middle term
steps.body:
6x² − 3 − 7x → write as 6x² − 7x − 3. Need two numbers with product 6 × (−3) = −18 and sum −7: −9 and 2.

6x² − 9x + 2x − 3 = 3x(2x − 3) + 1(2x − 3) = (3x + 1)(2x − 3). Zeroes: −1/3, 3/2. Sum = 7/6 = −(−7)/6 ✓, product = −1/2 = −3/6 ✓

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign in α + β = −b/a.
- Not rearranging into standard form (6x² − 3 − 7x has b = −7, c = −3).
- Writing zeroes of (x + 2) as +2 instead of −2.

activity.prompt: Fill in the relations for p(x) = 2x² − 8x + 6 (zeroes 1 and 3).
activity.text: Sum of zeroes = −b/a = ___ and product = c/a = ___.

quiz.q: Sum of zeroes of 3x² − 5x + 2 is
quiz.why: Sum of zeroes = −b/a = −(−5)/3 = 5/3.

quiz.q: Product of zeroes of 3x² − 5x + 2 is
quiz.why: Product of zeroes = c/a = 2/3.

quiz.q: Zeroes of x² − 2x − 8 are
quiz.why: x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2), so the zeroes are 4 and −2.

quiz.q: If one zero of x² − 6x + k is 2, then k is
quiz.why: Putting x = 2: 4 − 12 + k = 0, so k = 8.

quiz.q: If the zeroes of ax² + bx + c are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, then
quiz.why: Zeroes equal in size but opposite in sign add to 0. Sum = −b/a = 0, so b = 0.

quiz.q: Zeroes of 4s² − 4s + 1 are
quiz.why: 4s² − 4s + 1 = (2s − 1)², so 2s − 1 = 0 and s = 1/2 (twice).

lessons.title: Building a quadratic from its zeroes

scenes.text: Ananya wants a quadratic whose zeroes add to 1/4 and multiply to −1, for a class quiz.
She remembers: x² − (sum)x + (product), then clear fractions.
In two lines she has 4x² − x − 4. Reverse engineering is a common 2–3 mark question.

steps.title: The formula
steps.body:
A quadratic with sum of zeroes S and product P is

**p(x) = k[x² − Sx + P]**, where k is any non-zero constant.

Choose k to clear fractions or roots so the answer looks neat.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — zeroes given directly: 2 + √3 and 2 − √3
Solved example 4 — symmetric expression
steps.body:
If α, β are zeroes of x² − 5x + 6, find α² + β².

α + β = 5, αβ = 6. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 25 − 12 = **13**. (Check: zeroes 2 and 3 → 4 + 9 = 13 ✓)

Similarly 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ = 5/6.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing x² + Sx + P (the middle sign must be minus).
- Forgetting 'k' — any non-zero multiple is also correct, so do not mark other students' 2x² − 2x … wrong.
- Computing α² + β² as (α + β)² without subtracting 2αβ.

activity.prompt: α and β are zeroes of x² − 7x + 10. Find α² + β².

quiz.q: A quadratic with sum of zeroes 0 and product √5 is
quiz.why: A quadratic is x² − (sum)x + (product). With sum 0 and product √5, it is x² − 0x + √5 = x² + √5.

quiz.q: Quadratic with zeroes −3 and 4 is
quiz.why: Sum = −3 + 4 = 1 and product = −3 × 4 = −12, so the polynomial is x² − x − 12.

quiz.q: If α, β are zeroes of x² + 3x + 2, then 1/α + 1/β is
quiz.why: 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ. For x² + 3x + 2, α + β = −3 and αβ = 2, so the value is −3/2.

quiz.q: Quadratic with S = 1 and P = 1 is
quiz.why: With sum 1 and product 1, the quadratic is x² − (1)x + 1 = x² − x + 1.

quiz.q: If α, β are zeroes of x² − 4x + 3, then α² + β² is
quiz.why: α + β = 4 and αβ = 3. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 16 − 6 = 10.

lessons.title: Going further: cubic polynomials and mixed problems

scenes.text: Dev's cubic 2x³ + x² − 5x + 2 has zeroes 1/2, 1 and −2.
His teacher asks him to check them using only the coefficients.
Cubics follow a similar pattern with three relations. This also prepares you for Class 11.

steps.title: Relations for a cubic (enrichment)
steps.body:
If α, β, γ are zeroes of ax³ + bx² + cx + d:

- α + β + γ = −b/a
- αβ + βγ + γα = c/a
- αβγ = −d/a

Boards following the rationalised NCERT book focus on quadratics; this is useful practice and is asked in some state boards.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — find k
steps.body:
If the sum of zeroes of kx² + 2x + 3k equals their product, find k.

Sum = −2/k, product = 3k/k = 3. So −2/k = 3 → **k = −2/3**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — difference of zeroes
steps.body:
If α, β are zeroes of x² − 8x + k and α − β = 2, find k.

α + β = 8, α − β = 2 → α = 5, β = 3, so k = αβ = **15**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing signs: for a cubic the product is −d/a, but for a quadratic it is +c/a.
- Dividing by k without noting k ≠ 0.
- Forgetting that one known zero lets you find the other quickly using the sum.

activity.prompt: Match each relation with its value for 2x³ + x² − 5x + 2.

quiz.q: For x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, the sum of zeroes is
quiz.why: For a cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d, the sum of zeroes is −b/a = −(−6)/1 = 6, which matches the zeroes 1, 2, 3.

quiz.q: For x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, the product of zeroes is
quiz.why: For a cubic, the product of zeroes is −d/a = −(−6)/1 = 6, which matches 1 × 2 × 3.

quiz.q: If one zero of 2x² − 3x + k is the reciprocal of the other, k is
quiz.why: If one zero is the reciprocal of the other, their product is 1. Product = k/2 = 1, so k = 2.

quiz.q: If sum of zeroes of x² − (k + 6)x + 2(2k − 1) is half their product, k is
quiz.why: Sum = k + 6 and product = 2(2k − 1). Sum is half the product, so k + 6 = 2k − 1 and k = 7.

quiz.q: If α, β are zeroes of x² − 8x + 15 and α > β, then α − β is
quiz.why: x² − 8x + 15 = (x − 3)(x − 5), so the zeroes are 5 and 3 and α − β = 5 − 3 = 2.

questions.q: Which is a quadratic polynomial?
questions.why: A quadratic polynomial has degree 2 with whole-number powers. x² − 3x + 1 fits, while √x and 1/x² are not polynomials.

questions.q: Zeroes of x² − 9 are
questions.why: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so the zeroes are +3 and −3.

questions.q: Number of zeroes of a polynomial whose graph cuts the x-axis at 4 points is
questions.why: Each point where the graph cuts the x-axis is a zero. Four such points mean 4 zeroes.

questions.q: Sum and product of zeroes of x² + 5x + 6 are
questions.why: For x² + 5x + 6, sum = −b/a = −5 and product = c/a = 6.

questions.q: A quadratic whose zeroes are 5 and −2 is
questions.why: Sum = 5 + (−2) = 3 and product = −10, so the quadratic is x² − 3x − 10.

questions.q: If one zero of x² + 3x + k is 2, k is
questions.why: Putting x = 2: 4 + 6 + k = 0, so k = −10.

questions.q: Assertion: x² + 4x + 5 has two real zeroes. Reason: every quadratic has exactly two real zeroes.
questions.why: The discriminant of x² + 4x + 5 is 16 − 20 = −4 < 0, so there are no real zeroes and the assertion is false. The reason is also false, since a quadratic need not have two real zeroes.

The zeroes of x² + px + q are double the zeroes of x² + 5x + 6. Then p and q are
questions.why: The zeroes of x² + 5x + 6 are −2 and −3, so double them: −4 and −6. Sum −10 = −p gives p = 10, and product 24 = q.

questions.q: If α, β are zeroes of x² − 5x + 6, then α² + β² is
questions.why: α + β = 5 and αβ = 6. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 25 − 12 = 13.

questions.q: Case: A bridge arch follows y = −x² + 4x − 3 (metres) across a stream along the x-axis. Where does the arch meet the water?
questions.why: Set −x² + 4x − 3 = 0, i.e. x² − 4x + 3 = (x − 1)(x − 3) = 0. So the arch meets the water at x = 1 and x = 3.

questions.q: For the arch in the case above, the sum of the zeroes equals
questions.why: Sum of zeroes = −b/a = −4/(−1) = 4, which agrees with 1 + 3.

questions.q: If α, β are zeroes of x² − x − 2, the quadratic whose zeroes are 2α and 2β is
questions.why: For x² − x − 2, α + β = 1 and αβ = −2. The new sum is 2 and the new product is 4 × (−2) = −8, so the quadratic is x² − 2x − 8.

questions.q: If α and β are zeroes of x² + 7x + 12, then 1/α + 1/β − 2αβ is
questions.why: For x² + 7x + 12, α + β = −7 and αβ = 12. So 1/α + 1/β = −7/12 and 2αβ = 24, giving −7/12 − 24.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
courses.summary: Represent two-variable situations as a pair of linear equations and solve them graphically, by substitution and by elimination; decide in advance whether there is one, none or infinitely many solutions.
outcomes: Learners can form a pair of linear equations from a word problem
Learners can solve a pair graphically and interpret intersecting, parallel and coincident lines
Learners can use ratio conditions to test consistency and find unknown constants
Learners can solve by substitution and elimination with full working
Learners can solve age, digit, fraction and cost problems

lessons.title: Forming equations and the graphical method

scenes.text: Akhila spent ₹20 at a fair: some rides at ₹3 each and some hoopla games at ₹4 each.
She took 2 more rides than games. Let x = rides and y = games: 3x + 4y = 20 and x − y = 2.
Two conditions give two lines. Where they cross is the answer. Graphs make the idea visible.

steps.title: What a pair looks like
steps.body:
General form: a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0.

Each equation is a straight line. Plot 2–3 points for each (make a small x–y table) and draw both lines.

- Lines **intersect** at one point → **unique** solution (consistent).
- Lines are **coincident** → **infinitely many** solutions (dependent, consistent).
- Lines are **parallel** → **no** solution (inconsistent).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — x + y = 5 and 2x − y = 4
Solved example 2 — parallel lines
steps.body:
x + 2y = 4 and 2x + 4y = 12. The second is 2(x + 2y) = 12, i.e. x + 2y = 6.

The lines x + 2y = 4 and x + 2y = 6 never meet → **no solution**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — triangle with the x-axis
steps.body: Draw x − y + 1 = 0 and 3x + 2y − 12 = 0. They meet at (2, 3). The first meets the x-axis at (−1, 0), the second at (4, 0). These three points are the vertices of the triangle formed with the x-axis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Plotting only one point per line — always use at least two, ideally three for checking.
- Reading the intersection loosely from a rough sketch; verify by substitution.
- Confusing coincident lines (same line) with parallel lines (never meet).

activity.prompt: Match the graph with the type of solution.
pairs: Lines lie on top of each other

quiz.q: Two lines that are parallel represent a pair that is
quiz.why: Parallel lines have no common point, so the pair has no solution. Such a pair is called inconsistent.

quiz.q: Solution of x + y = 5 and 2x − y = 4 is
quiz.why: Adding x + y = 5 and 2x − y = 4 gives 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 2. The lines meet at (3, 2).

quiz.q: x + 2y = 4 and 2x + 4y = 8 have
quiz.why: The second equation is twice the first, so both are the same line. A single line has infinitely many points, so there are infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: The graph of a linear equation in two variables is
quiz.why: A linear equation in two variables (degree 1) has a straight line as its graph.

quiz.q: Point (2, 3) lies on
quiz.why: Putting (2, 3) in x − y + 1 gives 2 − 3 + 1 = 0, so the point lies on that line. The other equations are not satisfied.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables)

lessons.title: Consistency: ratios of coefficients

scenes.text: Before drawing anything, Farhan's teacher asks: will these two lines meet?
Farhan compares the ratios of the x-coefficients, y-coefficients and constants.
One glance at three fractions tells him the answer — a guaranteed 1–2 mark question.

steps.title: The test
steps.body:
For a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0:

- **a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂** → intersecting → unique solution
- **a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂** → coincident → infinitely many solutions
- **a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂** → parallel → no solution

steps.title: Solved example 1 — classify
steps.body: 5x − 4y + 8 = 0 and 7x + 6y − 9 = 0: a₁/a₂ = 5/7, b₁/b₂ = −4/6 = −2/3. Not equal → **intersecting, unique solution**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — find k for infinitely many solutions
Solved example 3 — find k for no solution
steps.body:
x + 2y = 3 and 2x + ky = 5.

a₁/a₂ = 1/2 = b₁/b₂ = 2/k → k = 4. Check c₁/c₂ = 3/5 ≠ 1/2 ✓. So **k = 4**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Moving constants to the right side for some equations and not others — keep the same form for both.
- Forgetting to check the c-ratio when the question asks for 'no solution' vs 'infinitely many'.
- Sign errors: b₁/b₂ for −4y and 6y is −4/6.

activity.prompt: Classify each pair.

quiz.q: For a unique solution we need
quiz.why: A unique solution needs a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂. The lines then have different slopes and cross at exactly one point.

quiz.q: Value of k for which kx + 3y = 3 and 12x + ky = 6 have no solution:
quiz.why: For no solution, k/12 = 3/k ≠ 3/6. k² = 36 gives k = ±6. At k = 6 all three ratios equal 1/2 (coincident lines), while at k = −6 the last ratio differs, so k = −6.

quiz.q: 3x + 2y = 5 and 2x − 3y = 7 are
quiz.why: 3/2 ≠ 2/(−3), so a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂. The pair is consistent with a unique solution.

quiz.q: Lines y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x + 5 are
quiz.why: Both lines have slope 3 but different intercepts (1 and 5), so they are parallel.

quiz.q: If a pair is dependent, its lines are
quiz.why: A dependent pair has infinitely many solutions, which means the two lines coincide.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables)

lessons.title: Substitution method

scenes.text: Ishaan knows x − y = −1, so x is always one less than y.
He replaces x by (y − 1) in the other equation and gets a single-variable equation.
Solving one variable at a time is the heart of substitution.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. From one equation, express one variable in terms of the other (pick the easiest, coefficient 1 if possible).
2. Substitute into the **other** equation and solve for one variable.
3. Substitute back to find the second variable.
4. **Check** in both original equations.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — detecting infinitely many solutions
steps.body: x + 2y = 4 and 3x + 6y = 12. Substituting x = 4 − 2y: 3(4 − 2y) + 6y = 12 → 12 = 12, a true statement for every y. So there are **infinitely many** solutions. (If you got something false like 12 = 15, there would be no solution.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Substituting back into the same equation you used for step 1 (gives 0 = 0 and no information).
- Forgetting brackets: 2(y − 1) ≠ 2y − 1.
- Not checking the answer in both equations.

activity.prompt: Solve by substitution: x + y = 14 and x − y = 4. Enter the value of x.

quiz.q: Solve s − t = 3 and s/3 + t/2 = 6. The value of s is
quiz.why: Put s = t + 3 in s/3 + t/2 = 6: (t + 3)/3 + t/2 = 6. Multiply by 6: 2t + 6 + 3t = 36, so t = 6 and s = 9.

quiz.q: If substitution leads to 0 = 5, the pair has
quiz.why: If substitution gives a false statement like 0 = 5, the equations have no common solution, so the pair is inconsistent.

quiz.q: From x + 3y = 6, x in terms of y is
quiz.why: Subtract 3y from both sides of x + 3y = 6 to get x = 6 − 3y.

quiz.q: Solution of 2x + 3y = 13, x − y = −1 is
quiz.why: From x − y = −1, x = y − 1. Then 2(y − 1) + 3y = 13 gives 5y = 15, so y = 3 and x = 2.

quiz.q: Solve 0.2x + 0.3y = 1.3 and 0.4x + 0.5y = 2.3. Value of y:
quiz.why: Multiply both equations by 10: 2x + 3y = 13 and 4x + 5y = 23. Doubling the first gives 4x + 6y = 26; subtracting the second leaves y = 3 (and then x = 2).

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables)

lessons.title: Elimination method

scenes.text: Pooja sees 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x − 2y = 2.
She doubles the second equation so the y-terms become +4y and −4y.
Adding the equations, y disappears. Elimination is the fastest method for most board questions.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. Multiply one or both equations so that the coefficients of one variable become equal (or opposite).
2. Subtract (if equal) or add (if opposite) to eliminate that variable.
3. Solve, then substitute back.
4. If both variables vanish: a true statement → infinitely many solutions; a false statement → no solution.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — 3x + 4y = 10, 2x − 2y = 2
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Multiply the second by 2: 4x − 4y = 4.

**Step 2:** Add to the first: 7x = 14 → x = 2.

**Step 3:** 3(2) + 4y = 10 → y = 1.

**Answer:** x = 2, y = 1.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — symmetric coefficients
steps.body:
47x + 31y = 63 and 31x + 47y = 15.

Add: 78x + 78y = 78 → x + y = 1. Subtract: 16x − 16y = 48 → x − y = 3.

So x = 2, y = −1. A neat trick when the coefficients swap.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying only the left side of an equation.
- Subtracting when signs are opposite (you should add).
- Arithmetic slips with negatives: −(−6y) = +6y.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to solve 2x + y = 7, x − y = 2 by elimination.
items: Notice the y-coefficients are +1 and −1
Add the equations: 3x = 9
Solve: x = 3
Substitute: 3 − y = 2, so y = 1
Check in 2x + y = 7: 6 + 1 = 7 ✓

quiz.q: To eliminate y from 2x + 3y = 8 and 5x − 2y = 1, multiply by
quiz.why: Multiplying the first by 2 and the second by 3 gives 6y and −6y. Adding then eliminates y.

quiz.q: Solution of x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 is
quiz.why: Adding the equations gives 2x = 6, so x = 3 and y = 5 − 3 = 2.

quiz.q: If elimination gives 0 = 0, the system has
quiz.why: If elimination gives 0 = 0, the two equations represent the same line, so there are infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: Solve 47x + 31y = 63, 31x + 47y = 15: x + y equals
quiz.why: Adding the equations gives 78x + 78y = 78, so x + y = 1.

quiz.q: Solve 3x − 5y = 4 and 9x − 2y = 7: x is
quiz.why: Multiply the first by 3: 9x − 15y = 12. Subtract it from the second: 13y = −5, so y = −5/13. Then x = (4 + 5y)/3 = 9/13.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables)

lessons.title: Word problems: ages, digits, fractions and costs

scenes.text: At a stationery shop, 3 pens and 2 notebooks cost ₹110, and 2 pens and 3 notebooks cost ₹115.
Zara wants the price of one of each.
Name the unknowns, write two equations, solve, and answer in words. That is the recipe for every word problem.

steps.title: The 4-step recipe
steps.body:
1. **Let** the unknowns be x and y (state units).
2. **Translate** each condition into an equation.
3. **Solve** (elimination is usually fastest).
4. **Answer** in a sentence and check it fits the story.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — prices
steps.body:
Let a pen cost ₹p and a notebook ₹n. 3p + 2n = 110, 2p + 3n = 115.

Add: 5p + 5n = 225 → p + n = 45. Subtract: p − n = −5.

So p = 20, n = 25. **A pen costs ₹20 and a notebook ₹25.**

steps.title: Solved example 2 — ages
steps.body:
Five years ago, Nuri was thrice as old as Sonu. Ten years later, Nuri will be twice as old as Sonu.

Let ages be N and S. N − 5 = 3(S − 5) → N − 3S = −10. N + 10 = 2(S + 10) → N − 2S = 10.

Subtract: S = 20, then N = 50. **Nuri is 50, Sonu is 20.** Check: 45 = 3 × 15 ✓, 60 = 2 × 30 ✓

steps.title: Solved example 3 — fraction
steps.body:
A fraction becomes 9/11 when 2 is added to both numerator and denominator, and 5/6 when 3 is added to both.

Let it be x/y. 11(x + 2) = 9(y + 2) → 11x − 9y = −4. 6(x + 3) = 5(y + 3) → 6x − 5y = −3.

Solving: x = 7, y = 9. **Fraction = 7/9.**

steps.title: Solved example 4 — digits
steps.body:
The digits of a two-digit number add to 9, and 9 times the number equals twice the reversed number.

Number = 10a + b. a + b = 9; 9(10a + b) = 2(10b + a) → 88a = 11b → b = 8a.

So a = 1, b = 8. **Number = 18.** (9 × 18 = 162 = 2 × 81 ✓)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 'ten years later' as N − 10.
- For digit problems, using ab as a product instead of 10a + b.
- Giving x = 20 without saying what x represents.

a.text: A taxi charges a fixed amount plus a rate per km. 10 km costs ₹105 and 15 km costs ₹155. What is your first move?

choices.label: Let fixed charge = x, rate = y; write x + 10y = 105 and x + 15y = 155
Divide 105 by 10 to get the rate

a2.text: ₹10.50 per km would make 15 km cost ₹157.50, not ₹155. Something is missing. Try again?

b.text: How do you solve x + 10y = 105 and x + 15y = 155?

choices.label: Add them: 2x + 25y = 260
choices.feedback: Adding keeps both variables. Subtract instead.

end.text: Fixed charge ₹5, rate ₹10/km. A 25 km ride costs 5 + 250 = ₹255.

quiz.q: The sum of two numbers is 27 and their difference is 3. The larger is
quiz.why: Adding x + y = 27 and x − y = 3 gives 2x = 30, so the larger number is 15.

quiz.q: In 'ten years hence, A will be twice B', the equation is
quiz.why: In ten years both ages increase by 10, so A + 10 = 2(B + 10). Adding 10 on only one side would be wrong.

quiz.q: A two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b is
quiz.why: A two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b equals 10a + b, by place value.

quiz.q: Half the perimeter of a rectangular garden is 36 m and length is 4 m more than width. Width is
quiz.why: Half the perimeter is 36, so l + w = 36, and l − w = 4. Adding gives 2l = 40, so l = 20 and w = 16 m.

quiz.q: Price of 1 pen and 1 notebook from the story example is
quiz.why: In the story example a pen costs ₹20 and a notebook ₹25, so together they cost 20 + 25 = ₹45.

questions.q: A pair of linear equations with no solution is called
questions.why: A pair of linear equations with no solution is called inconsistent, because the lines have no common point.

questions.q: x = 2 and y = 3 is the solution of
questions.why: Putting x = 2, y = 3 in 2x + y gives 4 + 3 = 7, so it satisfies that equation. The other equations are not satisfied.

questions.q: For 2x + 3y = 5 and 4x + 6y = 10, the lines are
questions.why: All the ratios are equal: 2/4 = 3/6 = 5/10 = 1/2, so the lines coincide.

questions.q: The pair x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 7 has
questions.why: 1/2 = 1/2 ≠ 3/7, i.e. a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂. The lines are parallel, so there is no solution.

questions.q: Solve x + y = 10, x − y = 2:
questions.why: Adding gives 2x = 12, so x = 6 and y = 10 − 6 = 4.

questions.q: For what k does kx − y = 2 and 6x − 2y = 3 have a unique solution?
questions.why: A unique solution needs a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂, i.e. k/6 ≠ (−1)/(−2) = 1/2. So k ≠ 3.

questions.q: Assertion: 3x + 4y = 7 and 6x + 8y = 14 have infinitely many solutions. Reason: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: The second equation is double the first, so all ratios equal 1/2 and there are infinitely many solutions. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.q: If 2x + 3y = 12 and 3x − 2y = 5, then x + y is
questions.why: Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 3: 4x + 6y = 24 and 9x − 6y = 15. Adding gives 13x = 39, so x = 3 and y = 2, and x + y = 5.

questions.q: Case: A school canteen sells 2 samosas and 3 idlis for ₹70 and 3 samosas and 2 idlis for ₹80. The price of a samosa is
questions.why: Let a samosa cost s and an idli i. Adding the equations gives 5s + 5i = 150, so s + i = 30. Subtracting gives s − i = 10, so s = 20.

questions.q: In the canteen case, the price of an idli is
questions.why: From the earlier working s + i = 30 and s = 20, so an idli costs 30 − 20 = ₹10.

questions.q: The value of k for which 2x + 3y = 7 and (k − 1)x + (k + 2)y = 3k have infinitely many solutions is
questions.why: For infinitely many solutions 2/(k − 1) = 3/(k + 2) = 7/(3k). The first two give 2(k + 2) = 3(k − 1), so k = 7, and the third ratio is also 1/3.

questions.q: A father is three times as old as his son. After 12 years he will be twice as old. The son's present age is
questions.why: F = 3S and after 12 years F + 12 = 2(S + 12). Substituting gives 3S + 12 = 2S + 24, so S = 12 years.

questions.q: The sum of digits of a two-digit number is 12; reversing the digits increases it by 18. The number is
questions.why: a + b = 12. Reversing the digits increases the number by 9(b − a), so 9(b − a) = 18 and b − a = 2. Then a = 5, b = 7 and the number is 57.

questions.q: Lines 2x − y = 2 and 4x − y = 4 meet the y-axis at
questions.why: On the y-axis x = 0. 2x − y = 2 gives y = −2 and 4x − y = 4 gives y = −4, so the points are (0, −2) and (0, −4).

questions.q: Lines x − y + 1 = 0 and 3x + 2y − 12 = 0 with the x-axis enclose a triangle of area
questions.why: x − y + 1 = 0 meets the x-axis at (−1, 0) and 3x + 2y − 12 = 0 meets it at (4, 0). The lines meet at (2, 3), so the area = ½ × 5 × 3 = 7.5 sq units.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Quadratic Equations
courses.summary: Recognise and form quadratic equations, solve them by factorisation and by the quadratic formula, judge the nature of roots using the discriminant, and solve real-life problems on area, speed, numbers and ages.
outcomes: Learners can write a situation as ax² + bx + c = 0
Learners can solve by splitting the middle term
Learners can apply the quadratic formula and explain where it comes from
Learners can use the discriminant to find the nature of roots and unknown constants
Learners can solve word problems and reject impossible roots

scenes.text: A community wants a rectangular hall of area 300 m² whose length is 1 m more than twice its breadth.
If the breadth is x m, the length is (2x + 1) m, so x(2x + 1) = 300.
That is 2x² + x − 300 = 0 — a quadratic equation. Many design and motion problems lead to one.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **quadratic equation** in x is ax² + bx + c = 0 with real a, b, c and **a ≠ 0**.

A number α is a **root** if aα² + bα + c = 0. A quadratic equation has **at most two** roots.

Always expand and simplify before deciding: (x + 2)³ = x³ − 4 simplifies to 6x² + 12x + 12 = 0 — quadratic!

steps.title: Solved example 1 — is it quadratic?
steps.body:
(a) (x − 2)² + 1 = 2x − 3 → x² − 4x + 5 = 2x − 3 → x² − 6x + 8 = 0. **Yes.**

(b) x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) → x² + x + 8 = x² − 4 → x + 12 = 0. **No** (the x² terms cancel; it is linear).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — form the equation
steps.body:
The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306.

Let them be x and x + 1: x(x + 1) = 306 → **x² + x − 306 = 0**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deciding 'quadratic' before simplifying — x² terms may cancel.
- Forgetting the condition a ≠ 0.
- Leaving the equation as x(x + 1) = 306 instead of standard form.

statements.s: x² − 2x = (−2)(3 − x) is a quadratic equation.
(x + 1)² = 2(x − 3) simplifies to a quadratic.
x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) is quadratic.
statements.why: The x² terms cancel, leaving a linear equation.

statements.s: x³ − 4x² − x + 1 = (x − 2)³ is quadratic.

quiz.q: Which is a quadratic equation?
quiz.why: A quadratic equation has highest power 2. x² + 3x − 4 = 0 fits, while the others have degree 1, 3 or a negative power.

quiz.q: In ax² + bx + c = 0, which must be true?
quiz.why: In ax² + bx + c = 0, a must not be 0. Otherwise the x² term disappears and the equation is no longer quadratic.

quiz.q: Is x = 1 a root of x² − 3x + 2 = 0?
quiz.why: Putting x = 1: 1 − 3 + 2 = 0, so the equation is satisfied and x = 1 is a root.

quiz.q: A quadratic equation has at most
quiz.why: A quadratic equation has degree 2, so it has at most 2 roots.

quiz.q: Rectangle with length = 2 × breadth + 1 and area 528. With breadth x, the equation is
quiz.why: If breadth is x, length is 2x + 1. Area x(2x + 1) = 528 gives 2x² + x − 528 = 0.

scenes.text: Tanvi must solve 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 for a design task.
She looks for two numbers with product 2 × 3 = 6 and sum −5: they are −2 and −3.
Splitting −5x into −2x − 3x lets her factorise neatly. Practice makes this fast.

steps.title: Splitting the middle term
steps.body: For ax² + bx + c = 0: find two numbers whose **product is a × c** and whose **sum is b**. Split bx, group in pairs, take common factors, and use: if PQ = 0 then P = 0 or Q = 0.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — consecutive integers
steps.body:
x² + x − 306 = 0. Product −306, sum 1: numbers 18 and −17.

(x + 18)(x − 17) = 0 → x = 17 (reject −18, since positive integers are needed). **Integers: 17 and 18.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing both sides by x and losing the root x = 0 (e.g. in x² = 5x, the roots are 0 and 5).
- Sign errors when grouping: −3x + 3 = −3(x − 1), not −3(x + 1).
- Not rejecting negative answers for lengths, ages or counts.

quiz.q: Roots of x² − 3x − 10 = 0 are
quiz.why: x² − 3x − 10 = (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0, so the roots are 5 and −2.

quiz.q: Roots of x² = 5x are
quiz.why: x² = 5x gives x² − 5x = 0, i.e. x(x − 5) = 0. So the roots are 0 and 5.

quiz.q: Roots of 2x² + x − 6 = 0 are
quiz.why: 2x² + x − 6 = 2x² + 4x − 3x − 6 = (2x − 3)(x + 2). So the roots are 3/2 and −2.

quiz.q: Roots of 100x² − 20x + 1 = 0 are
quiz.why: 100x² − 20x + 1 = (10x − 1)² = 0, so the root is 1/10, repeated twice.

quiz.q: To split the middle term of 3x² + 11x + 6 you need numbers with product
quiz.why: To split the middle term we need two numbers whose product is a × c = 3 × 6 = 18 and whose sum is 11. They are 9 and 2.

scenes.text: Dev tries to factorise x² − 4x − 2 = 0 and cannot find nice integers.
His teacher reminds him of a formula that always works.
x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a gives 2 ± √6 in seconds.

steps.title: The formula and where it comes from
steps.body:
For ax² + bx + c = 0 with b² − 4ac ≥ 0:

**x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a)**

**Why:** divide by a, then complete the square: x² + (b/a)x = −c/a → (x + b/2a)² = (b² − 4ac)/4a² → x + b/2a = ±√(b² − 4ac)/2a.

This method of completing the square is how the formula is derived.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — no real roots
steps.body: x² + 4x + 5 = 0: b² − 4ac = 16 − 20 = −4 < 0. The square root of a negative number is not real, so there are **no real roots**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking b = 7 instead of −7 (keep the sign!), so −b = +7.
- Dividing only the √ part by 2a: the whole numerator is divided.
- Writing √(b²) − 4ac instead of √(b² − 4ac).

activity.prompt: Use the formula on x² − 5x + 6 = 0. Enter the larger root.

For 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, the value of −b is
quiz.why: In 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, b = −7, so −b = 7. This is the value used in the quadratic formula.

quiz.q: The formula is derived using
quiz.why: The quadratic formula is derived by completing the square on ax² + bx + c = 0 and solving for x. It does not come from the distance formula, BPT or Euclid's lemma.

quiz.q: Roots of x² + x + 1 = 0 are
quiz.why: For x² + x + 1 = 0, D = b² − 4ac = 1 − 4 = −3 < 0, so the roots are not real.

scenes.text: Can a rectangular park of perimeter 80 m have area 400 m²? And area 450 m²?
Length l, breadth 40 − l: l(40 − l) = 400 gives l² − 40l + 400 = 0, D = 0 → yes, a 20 m square.
For 450 m², D = 1600 − 1800 < 0 → impossible. The discriminant answers 'is it possible?'

steps.title: D = b² − 4ac
steps.body:
- **D > 0** → two distinct real roots
- **D = 0** → two equal real roots, each −b/2a
- **D < 0** → no real roots

steps.title: Solved example 1 — find k for equal roots
Solved example 2 — kx(x − 2) + 6 = 0
steps.body: kx² − 2kx + 6 = 0. D = 4k² − 24k = 4k(k − 6) = 0 → k = 0 or 6. k = 0 makes it non-quadratic, so **k = 6**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — mango grove
steps.body: Can a rectangular grove with length twice its breadth have area 800 m²? b(2b) = 800 → b² = 400 → b = 20 m, l = 40 m. **Yes** (D = 0 − 4(2)(−800) > 0 for 2b² − 800 = 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to reject a value of k that makes a = 0.
- Writing D = b² + 4ac.
- For 'real roots' the condition is D ≥ 0 (includes equal roots), not D > 0.

quiz.why: For 2x² − 3x + 5 = 0, D = 9 − 40 = −31 < 0, so there are no real roots.

quiz.q: For equal roots of x² − 2kx + 16 = 0, k is
quiz.why: Equal roots need D = 0: (−2k)² − 4(1)(16) = 4k² − 64 = 0, so k² = 16 and k = ±4.

quiz.q: If D > 0, the roots are
quiz.why: When D > 0, √D is a non-zero real number, so the formula gives two different real roots. D = 0 gives equal roots and D < 0 gives non-real roots.

quiz.q: For which k does x² + 4x + k = 0 have real roots?
quiz.why: Real roots need D ≥ 0: 16 − 4k ≥ 0, so k ≤ 4. At k = 4 the roots are equal, which is also real.

quiz.q: A park of perimeter 80 m can have area
quiz.why: Perimeter 80 m gives length + breadth = 40, and area is greatest for the 20 × 20 square, 400 m². So 400 m² is possible, but 450 m² and 500 m² are not.

scenes.text: A train covers 360 km at a uniform speed.
If its speed were 5 km/h more, it would take 1 hour less.
Time = distance ÷ speed gives 360/x − 360/(x + 5) = 1. Let us solve it fully.

steps.title: Recipe
steps.body:
1. Let the unknown be x (with units).
2. Use the relation in the story (area = l × b, time = d/s, age next year = x + 1 …).
3. Simplify to ax² + bx + c = 0.
4. Solve and **reject** roots that make no sense (negative speed, length or age).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — ages
steps.body:
The sum of the reciprocals of Rehan's ages 3 years ago and 5 years from now is 1/3.

1/(x − 3) + 1/(x + 5) = 1/3 → 3(2x + 2) = x² + 2x − 15 → x² − 4x − 21 = 0 → (x − 7)(x + 3) = 0.

**Rehan is 7 years old.**

steps.title: Solved example 4 — right triangle
steps.body:
The altitude of a right triangle is 7 cm less than its base and the hypotenuse is 13 cm.

x² + (x − 7)² = 169 → 2x² − 14x − 120 = 0 → x² − 7x − 60 = 0 → (x − 12)(x + 5) = 0.

**Base 12 cm, altitude 5 cm.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping the negative root as an answer for speed or length.
- Writing time = speed/distance.
- Not checking that the answer satisfies the original story.

items: Let the integers be x and x + 2
Write x(x + 2) = 63
Rearrange: x² + 2x − 63 = 0
Factorise: (x + 9)(x − 7) = 0
Reject −9; the integers are 7 and 9

quiz.why: Solving the quadratic gives two roots, and one is −45. A speed cannot be negative, so we reject −45 and keep 40 km/h.

quiz.q: A number plus its reciprocal equals 10/3. The positive numbers are
quiz.why: x + 1/x = 10/3 gives 3x² − 10x + 3 = 0, i.e. (3x − 1)(x − 3) = 0. So x = 3 or 1/3, and the numbers are 3 and 1/3.

quiz.q: Two numbers differ by 3 and their product is 504. One pair is
quiz.why: x(x + 3) = 504 gives x² + 3x − 504 = 0, i.e. (x + 24)(x − 21) = 0. So x = 21 and the other number is 24, and 21 × 24 = 504.

quiz.q: In word problems you reject a root when it
quiz.why: A root is rejected only when it makes no sense in the situation, such as a negative length or speed. Being prime, a fraction or larger is not a reason.

quiz.q: Base and altitude of the right triangle example are
quiz.why: The equation factorises as (x − 12)(x + 5) = 0. The negative value is rejected for a length, so the sides are 12 cm and 5 cm.

questions.q: Which is NOT a quadratic equation?
questions.why: x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) gives x² + x + 8 = x² − 4. The x² terms cancel, leaving the linear equation x + 12 = 0, so it is not quadratic.

questions.q: Roots of x² − 16 = 0 are
questions.why: x² − 16 = 0 gives x² = 16, so x = +4 or −4.

Roots of 2x² − x − 6 = 0 are
questions.why: 2x² − x − 6 = 2x² − 4x + 3x − 6 = (x − 2)(2x + 3). So the roots are 2 and −3/2.

questions.why: Putting x = 2: 4 + 2k − 6 = 0, so 2k = 2 and k = 1.

questions.q: Nature of roots of 3x² − 4√3x + 4 = 0:
questions.why: D = (−4√3)² − 4(3)(4) = 48 − 48 = 0, so the roots are real and equal.

questions.q: Assertion: x² + 1 = 0 has no real roots. Reason: its discriminant is negative.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: x² + 1 = 0 would need x² = −1, which no real number satisfies, so A is true. Its discriminant is 0 − 4 = −4 < 0, so R is true and explains A.

questions.q: Values of k for which 9x² + 3kx + 4 = 0 has equal roots:
questions.why: Equal roots need D = (3k)² − 4(9)(4) = 9k² − 144 = 0, so k² = 16 and k = ±4.

Case: A cottage-industry unit finds that the cost of each toy (₹) was 55 minus the number made in a day, and on one day the total cost was ₹750. The number of toys could be
questions.why: Total cost x(55 − x) = 750 gives x² − 55x + 750 = 0, i.e. (x − 25)(x − 30) = 0. So the number of toys is 25 or 30.

questions.q: Case continued: if 25 toys were made, the cost per toy was
questions.why: Cost per toy = 55 − number made = 55 − 25 = ₹30. Check: 25 × 30 = 750.

questions.q: A two-digit number is 4 times the sum of its digits and twice the product of its digits. The number is
questions.why: 10a + b = 4(a + b) gives b = 2a. Then 10a + b = 2ab gives 12a = 4a², so a = 3 and b = 6. The number is 36.

questions.q: A motor boat with still-water speed 18 km/h takes 1 hour more to go 24 km upstream than downstream. Stream speed is
questions.why: With stream speed s: 24/(18 − s) − 24/(18 + s) = 1 gives 48s = 324 − s², i.e. s² + 48s − 324 = 0, or (s + 54)(s − 6) = 0. So s = 6 km/h.

questions.q: For what k does kx² − 6x − 2 = 0 have real roots?
questions.why: Real roots need D ≥ 0: 36 + 8k ≥ 0, so k ≥ −9/2. Since the equation must be quadratic, k ≠ 0 as well.

questions.q: The perimeter of a rectangle is 28 m and its area 40 m². Its sides are
questions.why: l + w = 14 and lw = 40, so l(14 − l) = 40 gives l² − 14l + 40 = 0, i.e. (l − 10)(l − 4) = 0. The sides are 10 m and 4 m.

questions.q: If the roots of (a − b)x² + (b − c)x + (c − a) = 0 are equal, which relation holds? (Note x = 1 is always a root.)
questions.why: Product of roots = (c − a)/(a − b) = 1 since both roots are 1 → c − a = a − b → 2a = b + c.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Arithmetic Progressions
courses.summary: Recognise arithmetic progressions, find any term with aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, add up terms with Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d], and apply both to savings, production, prizes and stacking problems.
outcomes: Learners can identify an AP and its common difference
Learners can find the nth term, the nth term from the end, and test whether a number is a term
Learners can derive and apply the sum formula
Learners can find aₙ from Sₙ
Learners can solve real-life AP problems

scenes.text: Aarav's grandmother gives him ₹50 on his first birthday, ₹60 on the next, ₹70 after that…
The list 50, 60, 70, 80, … grows by the same amount each time.
Lists that climb (or fall) by a fixed step are arithmetic progressions.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
An **arithmetic progression (AP)** is a list of numbers in which each term after the first is obtained by adding a fixed number **d**, the **common difference**.

General form: a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, …

d = a₂ − a₁ = a₃ − a₂ = … (d may be positive, negative or zero).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — is it an AP?
steps.body:
(a) 4, 10, 16, 22, … differences 6, 6, 6 → **AP, d = 6**.

(b) 1, −1, −3, −5 → differences −2 each → **AP, d = −2**.

(c) 1, 4, 9, 16 → differences 3, 5, 7 → **not an AP**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing d as a₁ − a₂ (it is later term minus earlier term).
- Checking only one difference — check at least two or three.
- Assuming a growing list must be an AP (1, 2, 4, 8 doubles, it does not add).

activity.prompt: AP or not an AP?

quiz.q: Common difference of 3, 1, −1, −3 is
quiz.why: The common difference d = second term − first term = 1 − 3 = −2. It stays the same for every pair of consecutive terms.

quiz.q: Which is an AP?
quiz.why: In −10, −6, −2, 2 each term is 4 more than the one before, so d = 4. The other lists have a ratio or a changing difference.

quiz.q: If a = 10 and d = 10, the first four terms are
quiz.why: With a = 10 and d = 10, we keep adding 10: 10, 20, 30, 40.

quiz.q: The AP with all terms equal has d =
quiz.why: If all terms are equal, nothing is added from term to term, so d = 0.

In which year will his salary reach ₹7000?
7000 = 5000 + (n − 1)200 gives n = 11. One formula answers it.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**aₙ = a + (n − 1)d**, where a is the first term and d the common difference.

nth term from the **end** of an AP with last term l: **l − (n − 1)d**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — is 301 a term of 5, 11, 17, 23, …?
steps.body: 301 = 5 + (n − 1)6 → n − 1 = 296/6 = 49.33… Not a whole number, so **301 is not a term**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — how many three-digit numbers are divisible by 7?
Solved example 5 — two conditions
steps.body: The 3rd term is 16 and the 7th term exceeds the 5th by 12. Then 2d = 12 → d = 6 and a + 2d = 16 → a = 4. **AP: 4, 10, 16, 22, …**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a + nd instead of a + (n − 1)d.
- Accepting a fractional n — n must be a natural number.
- For the term from the end, subtracting from l (or reverse the AP and use d → −d).

quiz.why: The two-digit multiples of 3 are 12, 15, …, 99. Their number is (99 − 12)/3 + 1 = 29 + 1 = 30.

quiz.why: aₙ₊₁ − aₙ = [3 + 4(n + 1)] − [3 + 4n] = 4, so the common difference is 4.

quiz.q: The year when the salary in the story reaches ₹7000 is the
quiz.why: The salary reaches ₹7000 when n − 1 = 10, so n = 11. The salary in year 1 is the first term, so it is the 11th year.

lessons.title: Sum of the first n terms

scenes.text: A famous story: a schoolboy was asked to add 1 + 2 + … + 100.
He paired 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98 … — every pair makes 101, and there are 50 pairs.
5050 in seconds! The same pairing idea gives the AP sum formula.

steps.title: Formula and derivation
steps.body:
S = a + (a + d) + … + [a + (n − 1)d]. Write it again in reverse and add the two lines term by term: each pair sums to 2a + (n − 1)d and there are n pairs, so 2S = n[2a + (n − 1)d].

**Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2 (a + l)**, where l is the last term.

Also **aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — sum of 22 terms of 8, 3, −2, …
Solved example 2 — first n natural numbers and odd numbers
Solved example 3 — how many terms give a sum?
Solved example 4 — aₙ from Sₙ
steps.body: If Sₙ = 4n − n², then a₁ = S₁ = 3, S₂ = 4, so a₂ = 1, and aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ = **5 − 2n**. AP: 3, 1, −1, …

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using n(a + l) without the ½.
- Mixing up aₙ (one term) and Sₙ (total so far).
- Throwing away a valid second value of n without checking.

scenes.text: A factory made 600 TV sets in its 3rd year and 700 in its 7th year, with production rising by a fixed number every year.
The manager wants the 1st-year output, the 10th-year output and the 7-year total.
Two equations give a and d; then aₙ and Sₙ do the rest.

steps.title: Spotting an AP in a story
steps.body: Look for 'increases/decreases by the same amount every …'. Identify a, d and what n counts (years, rows, days). Decide whether the question wants **one term** (aₙ) or **a total** (Sₙ).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — prizes
steps.body:
₹700 is given as 7 prizes, each ₹20 less than the one before.

7/2[2a − 120] = 700 → 2a − 120 = 200 → a = 160. **Prizes: ₹160, 140, 120, 100, 80, 60, 40.**

steps.title: Solved example 3 — stack of logs
steps.body:
200 logs are stacked: 20 in the bottom row, 19 in the next, and so on.

n/2[40 − (n − 1)] = 200 → n² − 41n + 400 = 0 → (n − 16)(n − 25) = 0.

n = 25 would need rows with negative logs, so **16 rows**, top row has 20 − 15 = **5 logs**.

steps.title: Where APs appear
steps.body:
- Fixed EMI-free savings that grow by a set amount each month
- Seats in an auditorium increasing by 2 per row
- Taxi fares: fixed charge + rate per km (1st km, 2nd km …)
- Simple interest year by year (compound interest is NOT an AP)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking a = production in the 3rd year.
- Answering with n = 25 rows without checking the context.
- Treating compound growth as an AP.

pairs: Total when first and last terms are known
