lessons.title: Arcs and sectors

scenes.text: The minute hand of a wall clock is 14 cm long.
In 5 minutes it turns through 30° and sweeps a pizza-slice shaped region.
That slice is a sector; its curved edge is an arc. Both are fractions θ/360 of the full circle.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
For a sector of angle θ (in degrees) in a circle of radius r:

- **Arc length l = (θ/360°) × 2πr**
- **Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr²** (also = ½ × l × r)
- **Major sector** area = πr² − minor sector area.
- Perimeter of a sector = 2r + l.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — sector of 30°, radius 4 cm (π = 3.14)
Solved example 3 — car wipers
steps.body: Two wipers, blade length 25 cm each, sweep 115°. Total area = 2 × (115/360) × (22/7) × 625 = **1254.96 cm²** (approx.).

steps.title: Solved example 4 — lighthouse warning sector
steps.body: A lighthouse spreads red light over a sector of 80° to a distance of 16.5 km. Area = (80/360) × 3.14 × 16.5² = **189.97 km²** (approx.).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using θ/180 instead of θ/360.
- Forgetting to add 2r when the perimeter of a sector is asked.
- Using the minute hand's 5 minutes as 5°: the hand turns 6° per minute.

activity.label: Slide the sector angle for a circle of radius 7 cm (π = 22/7). Sector area = θ/360 × 154 cm².

bands.text: Small slice: up to 25.7 cm² (60° gives 25.67 cm²).
Most of the circle — a major sector.

quiz.q: Arc length of a 60° sector of radius 21 cm (π = 22/7):
quiz.why: Circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 21 = 132 cm. A 60° sector is 1/6 of it, so the arc is 132/6 = 22 cm.

quiz.q: Area of a quadrant of a circle of radius 14 cm:
quiz.why: Area of the full circle = (22/7) × 14² = 616 cm². A quadrant is 1/4 of it, so 616/4 = 154 cm².

quiz.q: Minute hand of length 14 cm: area swept in 5 min ≈
quiz.why: In 5 minutes the hand turns 30°, which is 1/12 of the circle. 616/12 ≈ 51.33 cm².

quiz.q: The angle turned by a minute hand in 1 minute is
quiz.why: The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, so it turns 360°/60 = 6° each minute.

quiz.q: Sector area can also be written as
quiz.why: Sector area = (θ/360)πr² = ½ × r × [(θ/360) × 2πr] = ½ × l × r, where l is the arc length.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Areas Related to Circles)

lessons.title: Segments of a circle

scenes.text: An arched window is a segment: the region between a chord and its arc.
The builder needs its area to order coloured glass.
Segment = sector minus the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Minor segment area = sector area − area of ΔOAB**, where O is the centre and AB the chord.

- If θ = 60°, ΔOAB is equilateral: area = (√3/4)r².
- If θ = 90°, ΔOAB is right-angled: area = ½r².
- If θ = 120°, area of ΔOAB = (√3/4)r² (drop a perpendicular from O: height r/2, half-chord (√3/2)r).

**Major segment** = πr² − minor segment.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — chord subtending 60°, r = 21 cm
steps.body:
Sector = (60/360)(22/7)(441) = 231 cm². Triangle (equilateral) = (√3/4)(441) ≈ 190.95 cm².

**Minor segment ≈ 40.05 cm²**. Arc length = (1/6)(2)(22/7)(21) = 22 cm.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — right angle, r = 10 cm (π = 3.14)
steps.body: Sector = 78.5 cm², triangle = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 cm². **Minor segment = 28.5 cm²; major segment = 314 − 28.5 = 285.5 cm²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to subtract the triangle (giving the sector instead of the segment).
- Using ½ × base × height with the radius as height for non-right triangles.
- Mixing π values within one problem.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the area of a minor segment.
items: Note r and the angle θ at the centre
Find the sector area (θ/360)πr²
Find the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord
Subtract: segment = sector − triangle
For the major segment, subtract the minor segment from πr²

quiz.q: A segment is the region between
quiz.why: A segment of a circle is the region between a chord and the arc it cuts off. A sector lies between two radii and an arc.

quiz.q: Minor segment for θ = 90°, r = 10 cm (π = 3.14):
quiz.why: Sector area = (90/360) × 3.14 × 100 = 78.5 cm². Triangle OAB = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 cm². Minor segment = 78.5 − 50 = 28.5 cm².

quiz.q: Area of triangle OAB when θ = 60° and r = 6 cm:
quiz.why: With θ = 60° and OA = OB = 6, the triangle is equilateral with side 6. Area = (√3/4) × 6² = 9√3 cm².

quiz.q: Major segment area =
quiz.why: The major segment is the rest of the circle after removing the minor segment, so its area = πr² − area of minor segment.

quiz.q: For θ = 120°, the triangle OAB has area
quiz.why: Area of triangle OAB = ½ r² sin θ = ½ r² sin 120° = ½ r² × √3/2 = (√3/4)r².

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Areas Related to Circles)

lessons.title: Designs and applications

scenes.text: A craftsman makes a circular brooch of diameter 35 mm from silver wire, with 5 diameters dividing it into 10 equal sectors.
How much wire? What is the area of each sector?
Design questions combine circumference, arcs and sectors.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Break the design into circles, sectors, segments, triangles and rectangles. Add the pieces you keep and subtract the pieces cut out. Keep exact π until the last step if possible.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — umbrella panels
steps.body: An umbrella has 8 equally spaced ribs; treat it as a flat circle of radius 45 cm. Area between two consecutive ribs = (1/8)(22/7)(2025) = **795.54 cm²** (approx.).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — grazing horse
steps.body: A horse is tied to a corner peg of a square field of side 15 m with a 5 m rope. Grazing area = quadrant = (1/4)(3.14)(25) = **19.625 m²**. With a 10 m rope: (1/4)(3.14)(100) = 78.5 m², an increase of **58.875 m²**.

steps.title: Where it shows up
steps.body: Fan blade sweep, sprinkler coverage, pizza slice pricing, race-track lanes, rangoli designs, the area a wiper cleans, and radar/lighthouse coverage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the extra straight pieces (diameters/radii) in wire problems.
- Treating a rope tied at a corner as a semicircle (it is a quadrant when the angle is 90°).
- Rounding intermediate values heavily.

activity.prompt: A sprinkler waters a sector of angle 90° and radius 14 m. Watered area? (π = 22/7)

quiz.q: Brooch wire length in the story:
quiz.why: The wire length in the brooch is the sum of the two parts: 110 mm + 175 mm = 285 mm.

quiz.q: Area grazed by a horse tied at a corner of a square field with a 7 m rope (π = 22/7):
quiz.why: A horse tied at the corner of a square field can graze a quarter circle. Area = ¼ × (22/7) × 7² = ¼ × 154 = 38.5 m².

quiz.q: Perimeter of a semicircular protractor of diameter 14 cm:
quiz.why: Perimeter = semicircle arc + diameter = πr + 2r = 22 + 14 = 36 cm, with r = 7 cm.

quiz.q: Each of 10 equal sectors of a circle of radius 7 cm has area
quiz.why: The circle's area is (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm². Ten equal sectors share it equally, so each has 154/10 = 15.4 cm².

quiz.q: Increase in grazing area when the rope grows from 5 m to 10 m (corner, π = 3.14):
quiz.why: Quadrant areas: ¼ × 3.14 × 100 = 78.5 m² (10 m) and ¼ × 3.14 × 25 = 19.625 m² (5 m). The increase is 78.5 − 19.625 = 58.875 m².

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Areas Related to Circles)

questions.q: Area of a circle of radius 14 cm (π = 22/7):
Area of a sector of angle θ is
questions.why: A sector of angle θ is the fraction θ/360 of the whole circle, so its area is (θ/360) × πr².

questions.q: Arc length of a semicircle of radius 7 cm:
questions.why: The arc of a semicircle is half the circumference: πr = (22/7) × 7 = 22 cm.

questions.q: If the perimeter and area of a circle are numerically equal, the radius is
questions.why: 2πr = πr² gives r = 2 after dividing both sides by πr.

questions.q: Area of a quadrant of a circle with circumference 22 cm:
questions.why: Circumference 22 = 2πr gives r = 7/2. Quadrant area = ¼ × (22/7) × (49/4) = 77/8 cm².

questions.q: Assertion: The area of a sector of 90° is one-quarter of the circle. Reason: 90/360 = 1/4.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A 90° sector is 90/360 = 1/4 of the circle, so both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre. Minor segment area (π = 3.14):
questions.why: Sector = ¼ × 3.14 × 100 = 78.5 cm² and triangle = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 cm². Minor segment = 78.5 − 50 = 28.5 cm².

questions.q: The length of the minute hand is 7 cm. Area swept in 15 minutes (π = 22/7):
questions.why: In 15 minutes the minute hand turns 90°, a quarter circle. Area = ¼ × (22/7) × 49 = 38.5 cm².

questions.q: Case: A pizza of diameter 28 cm is cut into 8 equal slices. Area of each slice (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The pizza has r = 14 cm, so its area is (22/7) × 196 = 616 cm². Each of 8 equal slices has 616/8 = 77 cm².

questions.q: Case continued: the crust length (arc) of each slice is
questions.why: Circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 14 = 88 cm. Each of the 8 slices has an arc of 88/8 = 11 cm.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.35 m makes how many revolutions to cover 1.1 km? (π = 22/7)
questions.why: Circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 0.35 = 2.2 m. Revolutions = 1100 m ÷ 2.2 m = 500.

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 12 cm subtends 120°. Segment area (π = 3.14, √3 = 1.73):
Area of the region between a square of side 14 cm and the largest circle inside it (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The largest circle in a square of side 14 has r = 7, so area 154 cm². The square is 196 cm², so the leftover region is 196 − 154 = 42 cm².

questions.q: Two circles touch internally; the sum of their areas is 116π cm² and the distance between centres is 6 cm. Their radii are
questions.why: Touching internally gives R − r = 6, and R² + r² = 116 (π cancels). Trying R = 10, r = 4: 10 − 4 = 6 and 100 + 16 = 116.

questions.q: A sector of a circle of radius 21 cm has perimeter 64 cm. Its area is
questions.why: Perimeter = 2r + arc, so arc = 64 − 42 = 22 cm. Area = ½ × arc × r = ½ × 22 × 21 = 231 cm².

courses.title: Ch 12 · Surface Areas and Volumes
courses.summary: Surface areas and volumes of solids made by combining cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres and hemispheres — toys, capsules, tents, pen stands and sweets — with every formula and step shown.
outcomes: Learners can recall CSA, TSA and volume formulas of the basic solids
Learners can decide which surfaces are visible when solids are joined
Learners can find surface areas of combined solids
Learners can find volumes of combined and hollowed solids
Learners can solve cost and capacity problems

lessons.title: The formula toolkit

scenes.text: Lata's kitchen has a tin (cylinder), an ice-cream cone, a ball of dough (sphere) and a bowl (hemisphere).
To wrap or fill each one, she needs surface area or volume.
Before combining solids, let us lay out every formula once, neatly.

steps.title: Formula sheet (r radius, h height, l slant height)
steps.body:
- **Cuboid:** TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl), V = lbh
- **Cube (side a):** TSA = 6a², V = a³
- **Cylinder:** CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r + h), V = πr²h
- **Cone:** l = √(r² + h²), CSA = πrl, TSA = πr(l + r), V = ⅓πr²h
- **Sphere:** SA = 4πr², V = (4/3)πr³
- **Hemisphere:** CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr², V = (2/3)πr³

steps.title: Solved example 2 — hemisphere bowl
steps.body: Inner radius 10.5 cm. Capacity = (2/3)(22/7)(10.5)³ = **2425.5 cm³** ≈ 2.43 litres (1000 cm³ = 1 L).

steps.title: Units
steps.body: Areas in square units, volumes in cubic units. 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 L = 1000 cm³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the height h instead of slant height l in πrl.
- Using 3πr² (hemisphere TSA) when only the curved surface is exposed.
- Forgetting to convert diameter to radius.

activity.prompt: Match each solid with its volume formula.

quiz.q: CSA of a cone is
quiz.why: The curved surface area of a cone is πrl, where l is the slant height. πr(l + r) is the total surface area, which includes the base.

quiz.q: Slant height of a cone with r = 6, h = 8:
Volume of a sphere of radius 3 cm:
quiz.why: Volume = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π × 27 = 36π cm³.

quiz.q: TSA of a solid hemisphere of radius r:
quiz.why: A solid hemisphere has a curved surface of 2πr² and a flat circular base of πr², so TSA = 3πr².

quiz.q: 1 m³ equals
quiz.why: 1 m³ = 100 × 100 × 100 cm³ = 10,00,000 cm³, and 1 litre = 1000 cm³, so 1 m³ = 1000 litres.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

lessons.title: Surface area of combined solids

scenes.text: Rasika has a toy: a cone sitting on a hemisphere, both of radius 3.5 cm, total height 5 cm.
She wants to paint it. Which surfaces get paint?
Only the outside: the cone's curved surface and the hemisphere's curved surface. The joined circles are hidden.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: When solids are joined, the **surface area of the combination = sum of the exposed surfaces**. Joined faces are hidden and must not be counted. Often: TSA = CSA of part 1 + CSA of part 2 (+ any exposed flat faces).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — cube with hemisphere on top
steps.body: Cube side 7 cm, hemisphere of diameter 7 cm on top. Exposed = cube TSA − circle (covered) + hemisphere CSA = 6(49) − πr² + 2πr² = 294 + πr² = 294 + 38.5 = **332.5 cm²**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — capsule
steps.body:
A capsule is a cylinder with two hemispherical ends: total length 14 mm, diameter 5 mm. r = 2.5, cylinder length = 14 − 5 = 9 mm.

SA = 2πrh + 4πr² = 2π(2.5)(9) + 4π(6.25) = 45π + 25π = 70π = **220 mm²**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — tent canvas
steps.body: A tent is a cylinder (height 2.1 m, diameter 4 m) topped by a cone of slant height 2.8 m. Canvas = 2πrh + πrl = 2(22/7)(2)(2.1) + (22/7)(2)(2.8) = 26.4 + 17.6 = **44 m²**. At ₹500/m², cost = ₹22,000. (The floor is not covered.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the TSA of both solids (counts hidden faces twice).
- Forgetting the flat ring/circle that remains exposed (cube top minus hemisphere base).
- Using total length as the cylinder length in a capsule.

activity.prompt: For a cone on top of a cylinder (toy), which surfaces are painted?

quiz.q: Capsule surface area in the example:
quiz.why: The capsule's surface is made of a cylinder's curved part and two hemispheres. Putting in the given measurements gives 70π ≈ 220 mm².

quiz.q: For a cube with a hemisphere on top, the extra area beyond the cube's TSA is
quiz.why: A hemisphere on a cube hides a circle (πr²) of the cube's top but adds a curved surface of 2πr². The net change is −πr² + 2πr² = πr².

quiz.q: Tent canvas area in the example:
quiz.why: The tent canvas is the cylinder's curved area plus the cone's curved area: 26.4 + 17.6 = 44 m².

quiz.q: Combined solids' surface area counts
quiz.why: For combined solids, only exposed surfaces are counted. Faces where the solids join are hidden and left out.

quiz.q: A wooden article is a cylinder (h = 10, r = 3.5) with a hemisphere scooped out of each end. Its TSA is
quiz.why: The TSA is the cylinder's curved area plus the inner curved areas of two hemispheres: 2πrh + 4πr² = 220 + 154 = 374 cm².

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

lessons.title: Volume of combined solids

scenes.text: A sweet shop makes 45 gulab jamuns, each shaped like a cylinder with two hemispherical ends, 5 cm long and 2.8 cm across.
Each contains syrup equal to 30% of its volume.
Volumes simply add (or subtract for hollows) — no hidden-face worry here.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: **Volume of a combination = sum of volumes of the parts.** For a solid with a hole or scoop, **subtract** the removed volume.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — pen stand
steps.body:
A cuboid 15 cm × 10 cm × 3.5 cm has four conical depressions, each radius 0.5 cm, depth 1.4 cm.

Wood = 525 − 4 × ⅓(22/7)(0.25)(1.4) = 525 − 1.47 = **523.53 cm³**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — cone on hemisphere
steps.body: Radius 1 cm, cone height 1 cm. V = (2/3)π(1)³ + ⅓π(1)²(1) = π ≈ **3.14 cm³**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — vessel
steps.body:
A vessel is a hemispherical bowl of radius 7 cm topped by a cylinder of the same radius, total height 13 cm. Cylinder height = 6 cm.

V = (2/3)(22/7)(343) + (22/7)(49)(6) = 718.67 + 924 = **1642.67 cm³** (approx.).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting surface areas when volumes are needed.
- Using total height of the vessel for the cylinder part.
- Forgetting to multiply by the number of objects.

activity.prompt: A solid is a cylinder (r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm) with a cone of the same radius and height 6 cm on top. Find its volume (π = 22/7).

quiz.q: Volume of cone on hemisphere (r = h = 1 cm):
quiz.why: Hemisphere = (2/3)π(1)³ = 2π/3 and cone = (1/3)π(1)²(1) = π/3. Together they give π cm³.

quiz.q: Pen stand wood volume ≈
quiz.why: Volume of the wood = volume of the cuboid minus the volumes of the depressions scooped out. That works out to about 523.53 cm³.

quiz.q: Volume of a combined solid is found by
quiz.why: The volume of a combined solid is the sum of the volumes of its parts. Surface areas do not simply add.

quiz.q: A cylinder with a cone scooped out (same r and h) has remaining volume
quiz.why: Cylinder πr²h minus cone (1/3)πr²h leaves (2/3)πr²h.

quiz.q: Syrup in 45 gulab jamuns ≈
quiz.why: The syrup is 30% of the total volume of the gulab jamuns, which is about 0.3 × 1127.4 ≈ 338 cm³.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

lessons.title: Problem solving: cost, capacity and design

story.title: The water tank on the roof

scenes.text: A building's tank is a cylinder with a hemispherical bottom.
The plumber needs its capacity; the painter needs its outer area.
Real problems ask both — read carefully which one is wanted.

steps.title: Checklist for any problem
steps.body:
1. Sketch and label each part with r, h, l.
2. Decide: **area** (painting, wrapping, canvas, polishing) or **volume** (capacity, material, liquid)?
3. For area: list exposed surfaces only. For volume: add or subtract parts.
4. Convert units and compute cost = area × rate (or volume × rate).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — birdbath
steps.body: A birdbath is a cylinder (h = 1.45 m, r = 30 cm) with a hemispherical depression at the top. Outer + inner surface: 2πrh + 2πr² = 2π(0.3)(1.45 + 0.3) = 2(22/7)(0.3)(1.75) = **3.3 m²**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — cost of polishing
steps.body: A wooden article is a cylinder 10 cm tall, r = 3.5 cm, with hemispherical scoops at both ends is polished at ₹0.10 per cm². Area = 374 cm² (from the earlier lesson). **Cost = ₹37.40**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — ice-cream in cones
steps.body: A cylinder of ice-cream (r = 6 cm, h = 15 cm) is filled into cones of radius 3 cm and height 12 cm topped with a hemisphere. Each cone holds ⅓π(9)(12) + (2/3)π(27) = 36π + 18π = 54π. Cylinder = π(36)(15) = 540π. **Number of cones = 10**.

steps.title: Everyday uses
steps.body: Paint needed for water tanks, cloth for tents, metal for pipes, number of bricks for a wall, capacity of a pressure cooker or a petrol tanker — all use these formulas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Answering capacity in cm³ when litres are asked.
- Forgetting that a hollow (open) object has no top face to paint.
- Computing cost with area in cm² but rate per m².

activity.prompt: Before writing your final answer, check that you:
items: Converted all lengths to the same unit
Used radius, not diameter
Counted only exposed surfaces for area
Added/subtracted volumes correctly
Wrote units (cm², cm³, litres)
Rounded only at the last step

quiz.q: Painting a tank asks for
quiz.why: Painting covers the outside of the tank, so we need surface area, not volume.

quiz.q: Birdbath total area in the example:
quiz.why: The birdbath is a cylinder with a hemisphere's surface, giving total area 2πr(h + r), which comes to 3.3 m² for the given values.

quiz.q: Number of ice-cream cones in example 3:
quiz.why: Volume of the cylinder ÷ volume of one cone = 540π ÷ 54π = 10 cones.

quiz.q: 1 litre equals
quiz.why: Conversion.

quiz.q: Cost of polishing 374 cm² at ₹0.10 per cm²:

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

questions.q: Volume of a cylinder is
questions.why: The volume of a cylinder is πr²h, the base area times height.

questions.q: CSA of a hemisphere of radius 7 cm (π = 22/7):
questions.why: Curved surface area of a hemisphere = 2πr² = 2 × (22/7) × 49 = 308 cm².

questions.q: A cone and a cylinder have the same r and h. Ratio of their volumes is
questions.why: Cone volume = (1/3)πr²h and cylinder volume = πr²h, so the ratio is 1 : 3.

questions.q: Surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm:
questions.why: Surface area = 4πr² = 4 × (22/7) × 49 = 616 cm².

questions.q: Two cubes of side 4 cm are joined end to end. TSA of the cuboid formed:
questions.why: Joined end to end, the cubes form a cuboid 8 × 4 × 4. TSA = 2(32 + 16 + 32) = 160 cm².

questions.q: Assertion: When two solids are joined, the TSA of the combination is the sum of their TSAs. Reason: Joined faces become hidden.
questions.why: When solids are joined, the faces that touch are hidden, so they are not part of the TSA. Hence A is false and R is true.

questions.q: A toy is a cone of radius 3.5 cm on a hemisphere of the same radius. Total height 15.5 cm. Its TSA (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The cone has height 15.5 − 3.5 = 12, so slant height l = √(3.5² + 12²) = 12.5. TSA = πrl + 2πr² = 11 × (12.5 + 7) = 11 × 19.5 = 214.5 cm².

questions.q: Volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm:
questions.why: Volume of a hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π × 27 = 18π cm³.

questions.q: Case: A juice seller uses a cylindrical glass of inner diameter 5 cm and height 10 cm, but its bottom has a raised hemisphere of radius 2.5 cm. Apparent capacity (π = 3.14):
questions.why: The apparent capacity ignores the raised hemisphere: π × 2.5² × 10 = 3.14 × 6.25 × 10 = 196.25 cm³.

questions.q: Case continued: actual capacity of the glass:
questions.why: The raised hemisphere takes up (2/3)(3.14)(15.625) = 32.71 cm³. Actual capacity = 196.25 − 32.71 = 163.54 cm³.

questions.q: A solid cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 5 cm has a cone of the same base and height 4 cm on top. Volume:
questions.why: The cylinder is π × 9 × 5 = 45π and the cone is (1/3)π × 9 × 4 = 12π. Total = 57π cm³.

questions.q: A medicine capsule is 14 mm long with diameter 5 mm. Its volume (π = 22/7) approximately:
questions.why: The capsule is a cylinder of length 14 − 5 = 9 mm and radius 2.5 plus a sphere. Volume ≈ 176.8 + 65.5 = 242.3 mm³.

questions.q: A hemispherical tank of radius 1.75 m is full of water. Water in kL (π = 22/7) is about
questions.why: Volume = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)(22/7)(1.75³) ≈ 11.23 m³. Since 1 m³ = 1 kL, the water is about 11.23 kL.

questions.q: A cylinder of radius 6 cm and height 15 cm of ice-cream fills cones (r = 3, h = 12, with hemispherical tops). Number of cones:
questions.why: Ice-cream in the cylinder is π × 36 × 15 = 540π. Each cone with its hemispherical top holds 36π + 18π = 54π, so 540π ÷ 54π = 10 cones.

questions.q: A cube of side 10 cm has the largest possible sphere carved out of it. Remaining volume (π = 3.14):
questions.why: The largest sphere has r = 5, so volume = (4/3)(3.14)(125) = 523.33 cm³. Remaining = 1000 − 523.33 = 476.67 cm³.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Statistics
courses.summary: Mean, mode and median of grouped data: the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods for the mean, the modal-class formula, cumulative frequency and the median formula, and how the three measures relate.
outcomes: Learners can find the mean of grouped data by three methods
Learners can find the mode of grouped data with the modal-class formula
Learners can build a cumulative frequency table and find the median
Learners can find a missing frequency from a given mean or median
Learners can use the empirical relation 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean

scenes.text: Mrs Iyer has the marks of 50 students grouped as 0–10, 10–20, …, 40–50.
She does not know each exact mark — only how many fall in each class.
Using the class mark (mid-point) of each class as its representative, she can still find the mean.

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body:
**Class mark** xᵢ = (lower limit + upper limit)/2.

- **Direct:** x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ
- **Assumed mean:** choose a (a middle class mark), dᵢ = xᵢ − a, x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ
- **Step deviation:** uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h (h = class width), **x̄ = a + h × Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ**

All three give the same answer; step deviation keeps numbers small.

lessons.title: Choosing a measure and the empirical relation

scenes.text: A housing society's incomes include a few very rich families.
The mean is pulled up by them; the median shows the typical family better; the mode shows the most common income.
Knowing which measure fits the question is part of the exam too.

steps.title: Which one when?
steps.body:
- **Mean:** uses every value; good for comparing totals and averages (e.g. average marks of two sections). Sensitive to extreme values.
- **Median:** the middle value; best when data are skewed (incomes, house prices).
- **Mode:** the most frequent value; best for 'most popular' questions (shoe size, family size).

**Empirical relation** (for moderately skewed data): **3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — use the relation

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

courses.title: Ch 14 · Probability
courses.summary: Theoretical probability of equally likely outcomes: sure and impossible events, complementary events, and full sample spaces for coins, dice, cards, balls, numbered discs and real-life cases.
outcomes: Learners can define outcome, event and theoretical probability
Learners can use 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 and P(E) + P(not E) = 1
Learners can list sample spaces for one or more coins and two dice
Learners can solve card, ball, disc and defective-item problems
Learners can avoid common counting errors

scenes.text: Before a match, the captain calls 'Heads!' as the coin spins.
Two outcomes are equally likely, and one of them is a win for the call.
So the chance is 1 out of 2. Probability turns 'chance' into a number between 0 and 1.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Experiment:** an action with well-defined outcomes (tossing a coin).
- **Outcome:** a possible result; **sample space:** all outcomes.
- **Event:** a collection of outcomes (getting an even number).
- If outcomes are **equally likely**, **P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of outcomes)**.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.
- **Sure event:** P = 1. **Impossible event:** P = 0.
- **Complement:** P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
- An event with only one outcome is an **elementary event**; the probabilities of all elementary events add to 1.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — one die
steps.body: P(getting a number greater than 4) = favourable {5, 6} / 6 = **1/3**. P(not greater than 4) = 1 − 1/3 = **2/3**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — sure and impossible
steps.body: With one die: P(number less than 7) = 6/6 = **1** (sure). P(getting 8) = 0/6 = **0** (impossible).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — complement
steps.body: If P(rain tomorrow) = 0.35, then P(no rain) = **0.65**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a probability greater than 1 or negative.
- Treating outcomes as equally likely when they are not (e.g. 'win, lose or draw' in a match are not automatically 1/3 each).
- Forgetting to simplify fractions.

statements.s: A probability can be 1.2.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
Getting 7 on a normal die is an impossible event.
The outcomes 'win', 'lose', 'draw' are always equally likely.
The probability of a sure event is 1.

quiz.why: A probability lies between 0 and 1, so a negative number like −1.5 cannot be a probability.

Aman lists all 36 ordered pairs (1,1) to (6,6).
Sum 7 appears 6 times — more than any other. Listing the sample space settles arguments.

steps.title: Sample spaces
steps.body:
- **Two coins:** HH, HT, TH, TT (4 outcomes).
- **Three coins:** HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT (8).
- **Two dice:** 6 × 6 = **36** ordered pairs. (1, 2) and (2, 1) are **different** outcomes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — two coins
steps.body: P(at least one head) = {HH, HT, TH}/4 = **3/4**. P(exactly one head) = 2/4 = **1/2**.

Solved example 4 — three coins
steps.body: P(exactly two heads) = {HHT, HTH, THH}/8 = **3/8**. P(at least two heads) = 4/8 = **1/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting (1, 2) and (2, 1) as one outcome — that makes outcomes unequal in likelihood.
- Listing 3 outcomes for two coins ('two heads, two tails, one each') — 'one each' is twice as likely.
- Forgetting doublets like (4, 4).

scenes.text: A magician shuffles a 52-card deck and asks Neel to pick one.
Neel wonders how likely he is to get a red king, a face card or a spade.
Knowing the deck's structure makes these easy.

steps.title: A deck of 52 cards
steps.body:
- 4 suits: ♠ spades, ♣ clubs (black); ♥ hearts, ♦ diamonds (red) — 13 cards each.
- Each suit: A, 2–10, J, Q, K.
- **Face cards:** J, Q, K → 12 in all. Aces: 4. Kings: 4 (2 red, 2 black).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — balls in a bag
steps.body:
A bag has 3 red and 5 black balls. P(red) = 3/8, P(not red) = **5/8**.

If it has 5 red, 8 white and 4 green: P(not green) = 13/17.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — defective items
steps.body: Of 144 ball pens, 20 are defective. P(a pen is good) = 124/144 = **31/36**.

steps.title: Solved example 5 — find a number from a probability
steps.body: A box has 12 balls, x of them black. P(black) = x/12. If 6 more black balls are added, P doubles: (x + 6)/18 = 2x/12 → 12x + 72 = 36x → **x = 3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting aces as face cards (they are not).
- Forgetting that 'red' includes both hearts and diamonds.
- Using 100 as the total when discs are numbered 1–90.

scenes.text: A school fair sells 1000 tickets; there are 5 prizes.
Ravi buys one ticket. His friend buys ten.
Ravi's chance is 5/1000 = 1/200. Real problems use the same counting — just read carefully.

steps.title: Reading a case
steps.body:
1. Identify the experiment and the **total** equally likely outcomes.
2. Identify the favourable outcomes — list them if small.
3. Use complements for 'at least' or 'not' questions.
4. Simplify and sanity-check (0 ≤ P ≤ 1).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — lottery
steps.body: P(Ravi wins a prize) = 5/1000 = **1/200**. P(not winning) = **199/200**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — leap year
steps.body: A non-leap year has 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 day, so P(53 Sundays) = 1/7. A leap year has 52 weeks + 2 days; the extra pair is one of 7 possibilities (Sun–Mon, Mon–Tue, … , Sat–Sun), 2 contain Sunday → **2/7**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — game of chance
steps.body: A spinning arrow can stop at 1, 2, …, 8 equally likely. P(odd) = 4/8 = 1/2; P(number > 2) = 6/8 = 3/4; P(number < 9) = 1.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — two-player meeting days
steps.body: Two customers each visit a shop on one day from Tuesday to Saturday (5 days), equally likely. P(same day) = 5/25 = **1/5**; P(consecutive days) = 8/25; P(different days) = **4/5**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming a leap year has 53 Sundays for sure.
- Using 5 instead of 25 as the total for two independent choices.
- Forgetting order: (Tue, Wed) and (Wed, Tue) are different outcomes.

lessons.title: Formula sheet I: Number systems and algebra (Ch 1–5)

scenes.text: The night before the exam, Kavya wants all algebra formulas on one page.
She writes them from memory, then checks them here.
Self-testing beats rereading. Try covering each box and recalling it.

steps.title: Real numbers
steps.body:
- FTA: every composite = unique product of primes.
- HCF = product of smallest powers of common primes; LCM = product of greatest powers of all primes.
- HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b (two numbers only).
- √p is irrational for prime p; rational ± irrational is irrational.

steps.title: Polynomials
steps.body:
- ax² + bx + c: α + β = −b/a, αβ = c/a.
- Quadratic from zeroes: k[x² − (α + β)x + αβ].
- α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ.
- Cubic: Σα = −b/a, Σαβ = c/a, αβγ = −d/a.

steps.title: Linear equations
steps.body:
- a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ → unique; a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ → infinitely many; a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ → none.
- Methods: graphical, substitution, elimination.

steps.title: Quadratic equations
steps.body:
- x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/2a.
- D = b² − 4ac: D > 0 two distinct, D = 0 equal (−b/2a), D < 0 no real roots.

steps.title: Arithmetic progressions
steps.body:
- aₙ = a + (n − 1)d; nth from end = l − (n − 1)d.
- Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2(a + l); aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.
- 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2; first n odd numbers sum to n².

steps.title: Top 4 algebra slips
steps.body:
- Sign of −b/a.
- HCF × LCM rule for three numbers.
- a + nd instead of a + (n − 1)d.
- Forgetting to check the c-ratio.

scenes.text: Rohit can never remember which side is 'opposite'.
He draws a tiny right triangle in the margin for every trig question.
Quick sketches turn formulas into pictures — and pictures are hard to forget.

steps.title: Triangles
steps.body:
- Similar: equal angles AND proportional sides.
- BPT: DE ∥ BC ⇒ AD/DB = AE/EC; converse holds.
- Criteria: AA, SSS, SAS (included angle).

steps.title: Coordinate geometry
steps.body:
- Distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
- Section (m₁ : m₂): ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)).
- Mid-point: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Centroid: average of three vertices.

steps.title: Trigonometry
steps.body:
- sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj; reciprocals cosec, sec, cot.
- sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = 1/√2, sin 60° = √3/2 (cos runs backwards); tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3.
- sin² + cos² = 1; 1 + tan² = sec²; 1 + cot² = cosec².

steps.title: Heights and distances
steps.body:
- Angle of depression from A to B = angle of elevation from B to A.
- Use tan for height–distance; sin/cos when a slant length (ladder, string) is involved.
- √3 ≈ 1.732, √2 ≈ 1.414.

steps.title: Circles
steps.body:
- Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact.
- Tangents from an external point are equal.
- Angle between tangents + angle at centre = 180°.
- Circumscribed quadrilateral: AB + CD = AD + BC.

steps.title: Top 4 geometry slips
steps.body:
- Wrong vertex order in similarity.
- m₁ paired with x₁ in the section formula.
- sin(A + B) ≠ sin A + sin B.
- Same side vs opposite sides in ship problems.

activity.prompt: Match each fact with its chapter tool.

quiz.why: cot 60° is the reciprocal of tan 60°, so tan 60° × cot 60° = 1.

If ΔABC ~ ΔPQR and AB/PQ = 2/3, then BC/QR =
quiz.why: In similar triangles all corresponding sides have the same ratio, so BC/QR = AB/PQ = 2/3.

quiz.q: Angle between tangent and radius at the point of contact:
quiz.why: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so the angle is 90°.

quiz.q: From 20 m away, a tower top is at 45°. Height:
quiz.why: Height = distance × tan 45° = 20 × 1 = 20 m.

lessons.title: Formula sheet III: Mensuration, statistics, probability (Ch 11–14)

scenes.text: These chapters carry many marks and are mostly formula-and-calculation.
Careful arithmetic matters more than tricks.
Revise formulas, then practise one problem of each type.

steps.title: Areas related to circles
steps.body:
- C = 2πr, A = πr².
- Arc = (θ/360) 2πr; sector = (θ/360) πr² = ½lr.
- Minor segment = sector − ΔOAB (60°: (√3/4)r²; 90°: ½r²).

steps.title: Surface areas and volumes
steps.body:
- Cylinder: CSA 2πrh, V πr²h. Cone: l = √(r² + h²), CSA πrl, V ⅓πr²h.
- Sphere: 4πr², (4/3)πr³. Hemisphere: CSA 2πr², TSA 3πr², V (2/3)πr³.
- Combined: area = exposed surfaces only; volume = sum (or difference).

steps.title: Statistics
steps.body:
- Mean: x̄ = a + h Σfu/Σf.
- Mode: l + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × h.
- Median: l + (n/2 − cf)/f × h.
- 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean.

steps.title: Probability
steps.body:
- P(E) = favourable/total (equally likely).
- 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
- Two dice: 36 outcomes; three coins: 8; deck: 52 cards, 12 face cards.

steps.title: Exam-day strategy
steps.body:
- Read all questions in the first 10–15 minutes; start with what you know best.
- Show steps: formula → substitution → answer with units.
- For case-based questions, read the case twice.
- Leave 10 minutes to check signs, units and calculations.

steps.title: Top 4 slips in these chapters
steps.body:
- Counting hidden faces in combined solids.
- Using the cf of the median class itself.
- Treating (1, 2) and (2, 1) as one outcome.
- Using θ/180 for sectors.

quiz.why: A 90° sector is a quarter of the circle. Full area = (22/7) × 196 = 616 cm², so the sector is 154 cm².

quiz.why: Volume of a cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × (22/7) × 9 × 7 = 66 cm³.

quiz.why: The median of grouped data is found using the cumulative frequency, to locate the median class and its cf.

quiz.why: There are 12 face cards, so 40 cards are not face cards. P = 40/52 = 10/13.

quiz.why: 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean = 17 + 40 = 57, so Median = 19.

school-c10-sanskrit.title: Class 10 Sanskrit · Board preparation
school-c10-sanskrit.description: Class 10 Sanskrit board preparation: active/passive/impersonal voice, compounds in depth, study notes on selected Shemushi lessons, a formula sheet and a full mock paper.

courses.title: वाच्य परिवर्तन · Active, passive and impersonal
courses.summary: Converting between कर्तृवाच्य, कर्मवाच्य and भाववाच्य, with passive stems and board-style practice.
outcomes: Learners can convert active to passive
Learners can form भाववाच्य sentences
Learners can pick the correct वाच्य form in context

story.title: Who did it vs what was done

scenes.text: रामः ग्रन्थं पठति (active).
रामेण ग्रन्थः पठ्यते (passive).

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: In **कर्मवाच्य**: कर्ता → तृतीया, कर्म → प्रथमा, verb gets **य** + आत्मनेपद ending and agrees with the कर्म (पुरुष, वचन).

steps.title: Common passive stems
steps.body: पठ् → पठ्यते · कृ → क्रियते · दृश् → दृश्यते · गम् → गम्यते · लिख् → लिख्यते · पा → पीयते · दा → दीयते · श्रु → श्रूयते · खाद् → खाद्यते

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- बालकः फलानि खादति → बालकेन फलानि खाद्यन्ते।
- अहं पत्रं लिखामि → मया पत्रं लिख्यते।
- त्वं गीतं शृणोषि → त्वया गीतं श्रूयते।
- छात्राः पाठान् पठन्ति → छात्रैः पाठाः पठ्यन्ते।

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Verb agreeing with कर्ता: 'बालकेन फलानि खाद्यते' ✗ (कर्म plural → खाद्यन्ते).
- Forgetting pronoun forms: अहम् → मया, त्वम् → त्वया, वयम् → अस्माभिः, सः → तेन, सा → तया.

अहं शये → मया शय्यते।

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: For **intransitive** verbs (no object): कर्ता → तृतीया; verb in **प्रथम पुरुष एकवचन** आत्मनेपद with य, always (भाववाच्य).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- छात्राः हसन्ति → छात्रैः हस्यते।
- त्वं तिष्ठसि → त्वया स्थीयते।
- वयं धावामः → अस्माभिः धाव्यते।
- सा स्वपिति → तया सुप्यते।

steps.title: Spot it
steps.body: No object + तृतीया कर्ता + verb ending -यते (singular) = भाववाच्य.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'छात्रैः हस्यन्ते' ✗ — भाववाच्य verb is always एकवचन: हस्यते.

quiz.why: No object.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — वाच्य परिवर्तन in a passage

scenes.text: A dialogue has 3 blanks; choose the correct वाच्य form.
Then convert 3 sentences yourself.

steps.title: Task A (choose)
steps.body: शिक्षकः — छात्राः! भवद्भिः किं ___ (क्रियते/करोति)? छात्राः — अस्माभिः पाठः ___ (पठ्यते/पठामः)। शिक्षकः — शोभनम्। मया अपि ___ (हस्यते/हसामि)।

steps.title: Task B (convert)
steps.body: (1) वयं चित्रं पश्यामः। (2) सः ग्रामं गच्छति। (3) बालकः शेते।

steps.title: Answers
steps.body: A: क्रियते, पठ्यते, हस्यते. B: (1) अस्माभिः चित्रं दृश्यते। (2) तेन ग्रामः गम्यते। (3) बालकेन शय्यते।

steps.title: Tip
steps.body: First check: is there an object? Yes → कर्मवाच्य. No → भाववाच्य.

courses.title: समास · Compounds in depth
courses.summary: All compound types with vibhakti-wise तत्पुरुष, नञ्, उपमान कर्मधारय, बहुव्रीहि, द्वन्द्व and अव्ययीभाव, ending with a passage lab.
outcomes: Learners can write विग्रह for every compound type
Learners can distinguish कर्मधारय from बहुव्रीहि
Learners can identify compounds in passages

scenes.text: 'राष्ट्ररक्षा', 'नीलगगनम्', 'चन्द्रमुखी'…
Know the विग्रह to understand meaning.

steps.title: Vibhakti tatpurusha
steps.body:
- द्वितीया: ग्रामगतः = ग्रामं गतः · शरणागतः = शरणम् आगतः
- तृतीया: मदोन्मत्तः = मदेन उन्मत्तः · हस्तलिखितम् = हस्तेन लिखितम्
- चतुर्थी: यूपदारु = यूपाय दारु · भूतबलिः = भूतेभ्यः बलिः
- पञ्चमी: चौरभयम् = चौरात् भयम् · वृक्षपतितः = वृक्षात् पतितः
- षष्ठी: राजपुत्रः = राज्ञः पुत्रः
- सप्तमी: शास्त्रप्रवीणः = शास्त्रे प्रवीणः

steps.title: नञ् तत्पुरुष
steps.body: अधर्मः = न धर्मः · अनुचितम् = न उचितम् · असत्यम् = न सत्यम् (अ before consonant, अन् before vowel)

steps.title: कर्मधारय
steps.body: विशेषण-विशेष्य: पीताम्बरम् = पीतम् अम्बरम् (the cloth) · उपमान: चन्द्रमुखम् = चन्द्रः इव मुखम्, घनश्यामः = घनः इव श्यामः

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: पीताम्बरम् (the yellow cloth) = कर्मधारय, but पीताम्बरः (he who wears it) = बहुव्रीहि.

scenes.text: चत्वारि आननानि यस्य सः — Brahma.
बहुव्रीहि always points outside the words.

steps.title: बहुव्रीहि
steps.body: पीताम्बरः = पीतम् अम्बरं यस्य सः (विष्णुः) · चतुराननः = चत्वारि आननानि यस्य सः (ब्रह्मा) · नीलकण्ठः = नीलः कण्ठः यस्य सः (शिवः) · महात्मा (as 'great-souled one') · प्राप्तोदकः = प्राप्तम् उदकं यं सः (ग्रामः)

steps.title: द्वन्द्व

lessons.title: शुचिपर्यावरणम् — the poem on a clean environment

scenes.text: The poet sees the city choked by smoke, noise and dirty water.
He longs for the village, rivers and green trees.

steps.title: About the lesson
steps.body: A modern Sanskrit poem (see the textbook for the poet's credit) about pollution in the city — air, water, noise — and a wish to return to nature. Refrain: **'दुर्वहमत्र जीवितं जातं प्रकृतिरेव शरणम्'** — life here has become unbearable; nature alone is the refuge.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- The city is full of vehicles' black smoke and noise.
- Water is not pure; food is adulterated.
- The poet prays for a few moments in a lonely green forest by a stream.
- Message: protect nature, reduce pollution.

steps.title: Exam-style answers
steps.body:
- प्रकृतेः शरणं कुतः? → नगरे जीवनं दुर्वहं जातम्, अतः प्रकृतिः एव शरणम्।
- कविः कुत्र गन्तुम् इच्छति? → कविः नगरात् दूरं हरिते वने, नदीनिर्झराणां समीपे गन्तुम् इच्छति।

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Translating 'शुचि' as 'holy' only — here it means **clean/pure** (शुचिपर्यावरणम् = clean environment).

activity.prompt: Questions students ask about the poem

items.a: Difficult to bear/carry — life in the city has become unbearable.

items.q: Why does the poet call nature a refuge?
items.a: Because pure air, water and peace are found there, unlike the polluted city.

items.q: What is the poem's message for us?
items.a: Reduce pollution, plant trees, protect water and live closer to nature.

quiz.why: Clean.

quiz.why: Nature.

quiz.q: The poem mainly criticises
quiz.why: Pollution.

quiz.q: 'दुर्वहम्' means
quiz.why: Hard to bear.

lessons.title: बुद्धिर्बलवती सदा — wit is always strong

scenes.text: A woman, Buddhimati, travelling through a forest with her two sons, meets a tiger.
She slaps her sons and says: 'Why fight over eating one tiger? Find another!' The tiger flees.
A jackal brings the tiger back — but she outwits them both.

steps.title: About the story
steps.body: From the story collection **शुकसप्ततिः**. Buddhimati (wife of Rajsingh) uses presence of mind to scare off a tiger and later a jackal who tied himself to the tiger's neck.

steps.title: Plot points
steps.body: 1) She travels to her father's house with two sons. 2) Sees a tiger; pretends her sons want to eat a tiger. 3) The tiger, frightened, runs; called 'व्याघ्रमारी' (tiger-killer). 4) A jackal laughs and persuades the tiger to return, tied to his neck. 5) Buddhimati scolds the jackal: 'You promised three tigers, why bring only one?' 6) The tiger flees in fear, dragging the jackal.

steps.title: Exam-style answers
steps.body:
- बुद्धिमती कुत्र गच्छति स्म? → बुद्धिमती पितुर्गृहं प्रति गच्छति स्म।
- व्याघ्रः किं विचार्य पलायितः? → 'व्याघ्रमारी काचित् इयम्' इति मत्वा व्याघ्रः पलायितः।
- Moral: बुद्धिः बलवती — intelligence beats strength.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling the jackal clever in the end — he is the one fooled; the hero is Buddhimati.

scenes.text: 'आलस्यं हि मनुष्याणां शरीरस्थो महान् रिपुः।'
Laziness is the great enemy living in our own body.

steps.title: Key subhashitas (meaning)
steps.body:
- **आलस्यं हि मनुष्याणां शरीरस्थो महान् रिपुः। नास्त्युद्यमसमो बन्धुः कृत्वा यं नावसीदति॥** — Laziness is man's great enemy within; there is no friend like effort, doing which one never suffers.
- **गुणी गुणं वेत्ति न वेत्ति निर्गुणः…** — Only the virtuous recognise virtue.
- **क्रोधो हि शत्रुः प्रथमो नराणाम्…** — Anger is the first enemy of humans.

steps.title: Exam-style answers
steps.body:
- मनुष्याणां महान् रिपुः कः? → आलस्यम्।
- उद्यमसमः कः नास्ति? → बन्धुः।
- अन्वय: मनुष्याणां शरीरस्थः महान् रिपुः आलस्यं हि (अस्ति)।

steps.title: अन्वय (prose order)
steps.body: Rearrange: subject → object → verb; supply अस्ति if missing.

scenes.text: The exam asks एकपदेन, पूर्णवाक्येन and भाषिक questions on lessons.
Practise on the three lessons.

steps.title: Questions
steps.body: 1) एकपदेन: प्रकृतिः किम् अस्ति? 2) पूर्णवाक्येन: व्याघ्रः कथं पलायितः? 3) 'उद्यमसमः' — विग्रह? 4) 'पलायितः' — प्रकृति-प्रत्यय? 5) 'आलस्यम्' इत्यस्य विलोमपदं पाठात् चिनुत।

steps.title: Answers
steps.body: 1) शरणम्। 2) बुद्धिमत्याः वचनं श्रुत्वा 'व्याघ्रमारी इयम्' इति मत्वा व्याघ्रः भयाकुलः भूत्वा पलायितः। 3) उद्यमेन समः (तृतीया तत्पुरुष)। 4) परा+अय्+क्त (पलायितः). 5) उद्यमः।

steps.title: Tip
steps.body: For भाषिक questions, quote the exact word from the lesson.

courses.summary: Formula sheet for all grammar, घटनाक्रम and error-correction practice, and a full mock paper.
outcomes: Learners can recall all grammar rules quickly
Learners can order story sentences

scenes.text: Riya puts every rule on one page.
Sandhi, samasa, pratyaya, vachya, samay, avyaya.

steps.title: Sandhi
steps.body: दीर्घ (same vowels) · गुण (अ+इ=ए, अ+उ=ओ, अ+ऋ=अर्) · वृद्धि (अ+ए=ऐ, अ+ओ=औ) · यण् (इ→य्, उ→व्, ऋ→र्) · अयादि (ए→अय्, ऐ→आय्, ओ→अव्, औ→आव्) · जश्त्व, अनुनासिक, श्चुत्व, ष्टुत्व · विसर्ग: सत्व, उत्व, रुत्व, र्लोप

steps.title: Samasa
steps.body: तत्पुरुष (2nd word main) · कर्मधारय (adj+noun / उपमान) · द्विगु (number) · द्वन्द्व (च) · बहुव्रीहि (yasya saḥ — someone else) · अव्ययीभाव (अव्यय first)

steps.title: Pratyaya
steps.body: क्त्वा/ल्यप् (having done) · तुमुन् (to do) · क्त/क्तवतु (past) · शतृ/शानच् (while doing) · अनीयर् (should be) · मतुप् (having) · तल्/त्व (-ness) · टाप्/ङीप् (feminine)

steps.title: Vachya & time
steps.body: कर्मवाच्य: कर्ता-तृतीया, कर्म-प्रथमा, verb-य+ते agreeing with कर्म · भाववाच्य: verb always -यते (एकवचन) · Time: सपाद (+¼), सार्ध (+½), पादोन (−¼)

scenes.text: Exam: arrange 8 jumbled sentences of a story.
And fix 4 wrong sentences.

steps.title: Method for घटनाक्रम
steps.body: Find the opening (एकदा, एकस्मिन्…), follow time words (ततः, तदा, अन्ते), and the cause → effect chain.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Jumbled: (a) ततः कपोताः मुक्ताः अभवन्। (b) एकदा व्याधः जालं प्रसारितवान्। (c) कपोताः जाले पतिताः। (d) मूषकः जालम् अकृन्तत्। → b, c, d, a.

steps.title: Corrections
steps.body: सा गच्छति स्म → ✓ · ते बालकाः पठति → पठन्ति · अहं विद्यालयं गच्छति → गच्छामि · रामः सीताम् सह → सीतया सह

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ignoring connectors like ततः, अनन्तरम् which signal order.

scenes.text: Full mock: 60 minutes on grammar + reading.
Then check against the answers.

steps.title: Section A (reading)
steps.body: Unseen passage: answer one-word, full-sentence and title questions (use the c9 passage method).

steps.title: Section B (grammar)
steps.body: 1) Split: नयनम्, नमस्ते. 2) Compound: राज्ञः पुत्रः → ? ; पीताम्बरः → विग्रह. 3) Suffix: गत्वा, पठनीयम्. 4) Passive: सः पत्रं लिखति. 5) Time: 3:30. 6) Fill अव्यय: ___ (where) गच्छसि?

steps.title: Answers to B
steps.body: 1) ने+अनम् (अयादि), नमः+ते (विसर्ग) 2) राजपुत्रः; पीतम् अम्बरं यस्य सः (बहुव्रीहि) 3) गम्+क्त्वा; पठ्+अनीयर् 4) तेन पत्रं लिख्यते 5) सार्धत्रिवादनम् 6) कुत्र

steps.title: Time plan
steps.body: Reading 15 min · Writing 15 min · Grammar 25 min · Revision 5 min.
